Introduction
Purpose
This report provides a comprehensive overview of the current humanitarian situation, focusing on both operational environment
factors and sectoral analysis. It aims to support informed decision-making for humanitarian partners and stakeholders.
About GANNET
GANNET is a Generative AI Initiative from Data Friendly Space, offering AI-powered tools built to make knowledge and real-time
information accessible to our community in a resource-efficient and ethical way. It provides tools such as the GANNET Virtual Assistant
and GANNET SituationHub to help humanitarian actors access, analyze, and utilize critical information for their operations.
GANNET SituationHub
The GANNET SituationHub is a generative AI-powered digital public good designed to identify and analyze humanitarian data from
thousands of trusted sources in real time. By transforming complex data into clear insights, it enables faster, more effective response
strategies and improved coordination among stakeholders.
GANNET Virtual Assistant
The GANNET Virtual Assistant is a verified chatbot designed for humanitarian quick decision-making. Built on cutting-edge Generative
AI and trained with humanitarian expert-reviewed data, it provides real-time information. The GANNET Virtual Assistant facilitates rapid
data access and synthesis for crisis response.
Methodology Overview
The Situation Hub's analytical process uses a structured Human-in-the-Loop workflow that combines automated analysis retrieval
through GANNET Virtual Assistant, DFS's AI-powered humanitarian assistant, with expert review by the DFS analysis team. GANNET
automates the extraction and generation of crisis-related insights based on structured prompts, which are aligned with a tailored
analytical framework. These outputs are then reviewed, validated, and refined by analysts to ensure accuracy, contextual relevance,
and operational utility. The workflow is organized into four key phases: planning and setup, ongoing operations, quality assurance, and
system evolution, ensuring a balance between speed and analytical rigor.
Planning, Setup & Quality Control
In the planning phase, analysts develop a contextualized analytical framework, largely based on the Joint Intersectoral Analysis
Framework (JIAF), and convert it into structured prompts for AI-assisted data extraction. These prompts are refined over time to
improve output quality. Data sources are vetted for reliability, and translations are reviewed for accuracy. Using a centralized Content
Management System (CMS), analysts review and curate AI-generated outputs, validate them against external sources, and make
refinements to enhance clarity and relevance. The CMS enables collaborative editing and version tracking, ensuring outputs align with
humanitarian needs.
Bias Mitigation
To minimize bias, the team diversifies data sources, cross-verifies information, and continuously evaluates the AI's performance.
Analysts are crucial in identifying and correcting inaccuracies, especially in automated categorization. Future improvements aim to
enhance source credibility checks and sentiment analysis, further strengthening the reliability of the Situation Hub's outputs.
Crisis Overview
The SituationHub landing pages use a standardized yet customizable template to deliver consistent, comprehensive crisis overviews.
These pages integrate static content with dynamic data from sources like ACLED and DTM via open APIs, enabling interactive visuals
with real-time updates. Regular reviews and verification with in-country partners ensure accuracy, while manual updates are used for
sources not connected to APIs.
Media Monitoring
The media monitoring process has evolved from a manual, list-based approach to an AI-assisted system integrated into the CMS. This
allows analysts to efficiently review, filter, and contextualize media narratives, while automation helps track emerging trends.
3
Overview
The following overview has been generated using the information available up to June 29, 2026. It provides a synthesized summary
and key insights into the crisis based on the most recent data accessible at that time.
Summary
Myanmar has been in crisis since 1 February 2021, when the military (Tatmadaw) overthrew the democratically elected government.
This coup sparked widespread protests and armed resistance, leading to a severe political, economic, and humanitarian crisis. The
military regime, known as the State Administration Council (SAC), has responded with brutal force, resulting in thousands of civilian
deaths and widespread human rights abuses. As of March 2026, approximately 3.7 million people are internally displaced across the
country—a dramatic increase from roughly 300,000 pre-2021—with cross-border displacement projected to rise toward 5.2 million in
2026.
In attempt to seek international legitimacy, the military held general elections in three phases over December 2025 and January 2026
for the first time since the coup. The overwhelming majority of seats were won by the pro-military Union Solidarity and Development
Party (USDP) and saw SAC chairman Min Aung Hlaing elected as president in April 2026. The elections have been widely denounced as
neither free nor fair. Despite the transition to a quasi-civilian presidency, armed clashes have continued in multiple parts of the
country, including Sagaing, Magway, northern Shan, Kayah, Kayin, Kachin, Chin, and Rakhine. The Arakan Army (AA) now controls all
but three of Rakhine State's 17 townships, while resistance forces including the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) have
consolidated influence across parts of central and southeastern Myanmar. The UN's 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan
(HNRP), released 10 December 2025, projects over 16 million people will require humanitarian assistance this year.
Recovery from the March 2025 earthquake remains slow, with an estimated 3.5 million tonnes of debris and reconstruction hampered
by insecurity, shortages of heavy machinery (43%) and labour (40%), and limited access. Many affected communities, particularly in
Magway, Sagaing, and Mandalay, continue to live in temporary shelters, while essential services remain disrupted. Approximately
24,200 houses were damaged (24% completely destroyed), and 132 health facilities were damaged—half in Mandalay.
The Rohingya crisis continues to worsen, with the junta's blockade of Rakhine preventing international aid delivery since late 2023,
leaving hundreds of thousands of IDPs with severely limited assistance. On 10 December 2025, a military airstrike destroyed Mrauk-U
General Hospital, killing at least 33 people and injuring 76-80—one of the deadliest attacks on healthcare in the conflict. Chronic
poverty now affects over 80% of the population; the World Bank projects GDP will contract 2.0% in FY2025/26 with inflation remaining
above 20%, and market disruptions have deepened food insecurity nationwide. The 2026 HNRP appeals for approximately $890 million
but reflects severely constrained funding and narrowed operational space, forcing agencies to prioritize only 2.6 million people with
the most severe needs for life-saving support.
Key Insights
1. Myanmar's humanitarian crisis continues to deepen amid persistent conflict, economic collapse, and the lingering impacts of the
March 2025 earthquake. An estimated 16 million people—nearly one in three citizens—are projected to require humanitarian assistance
in 2026, as conflict-driven displacement, natural disasters, funding shortages, and humanitarian access constraints exacerbate
vulnerabilities nationwide.
The 28 March 2025 earthquake remains a defining event in the humanitarian landscape. Official figures from SAC confirm 3,770 deaths
and over 5,000 injuries, with the Early Recovery Cluster reporting over 24,200 houses damaged (24% completely destroyed), 4,857
apartments affected, and 132 health facilities damaged. An estimated 3.5 million tonnes of debris blocks roads and markets, with
clearance impeded by shortages of heavy machinery (43%) and labour (40%). Nearly three-quarters of the most affected townships
continue to face critical shelter and livelihood gaps—64% of communities reported job losses and 30-31% reported damage to crops
and workplaces—while disrupted water systems (44% of groundwater sources contaminated) have fueled outbreaks of cholera and
dengue.
2. Following the junta-run general elections held over December 2025 and January 2026, as well as ceasefires between the regime and
some ethnic armed organizations in northern Shan, the number of armed conflict incidents has gradually decreased. Nonetheless, air
and ground offensives continue in the Central Dry Zone, as well as Rakhine, Chin, Kayah, Kayin, and Kachin States. The new
government's 100-day roadmap announced on 21 April 2026, which invites resistance groups to enter peace talks and to surrender,
have not been widely accepted. 
Between January and November 2025, the military conducted 2,165 airstrikes, up from 1,716 in all of 2024. On 10 December 2025, a
military airstrike destroyed Mrauk-U General Hospital in Rakhine State, killing at least 33 people and injuring 76-80—prompting UN,
WHO, and Amnesty International condemnation and calls for investigation as a possible war crime.
IDPs have reached approximately 3.7 million people as of March 2025, with projections indicating it could rise further through 2026. The
AA now controls all but three of Rakhine's 17 townships, while resistance forces have captured extensive border areas in the southeast.
Attacks on healthcare are widespread: Insecurity Insight recorded 1,815 attacks on health care between February 2021 and November
2025, with WHO verifying 67 attacks in 2025 alone. Access restrictions, including the junta's blockade of Rakhine since late 2023,
continue to endanger civilians—particularly Rohingya communities facing persistent protection risks, restricted mobility, and limited
access to aid.
3. Humanitarian access remains severely limited by insecurity and deliberate obstruction. The 2026 HNRP appeals for approximately
$890 million but reflects severely constrained funding and narrowed operational space, prioritizing only 2.6 million people with the
most severe needs at a cost of $521 million.
4
Partners reached some 6.3 million people at the end of 2025, but access constraints—including roadblocks, landmines,
telecommunications blackouts, and the Rakhine blockade affecting 600,000 IDPs—force reliance on low-profile, community-led
delivery modalities. WFP warns that hunger has reached "unacceptable" levels, with over 400,000 young children and mothers
surviving on nutrient-deprived diets of plain rice or watery porridge.
4. The Food Security Cluster estimates about 12 million people face moderate-to-severe food insecurity in 2026, driven by conflict,
displacement, rising food and fuel prices, reduced market access and supply-chain disruptions. September 2025 analyses reported
"Serious" to "Critical" Global Acute Malnutrition in multiple conflict-affected townships, notably in northern Rakhine, Kachin, Sagaing,
southern Shan, and Kayah—with nutrition and treatment services suspended or operating at minimal capacity due to access
constraints.
Economic conditions continue to deteriorate: the World Bank projects real GDP will contract 2.0% in FY2025/26, with inflation remaining
above 20%. Rising poverty and fear of forced conscription have driven male migration, leaving women, girls, and older people as
household heads. More than four in ten households identify lack of income as their top challenge, and 83% of internally displaced
families can meet half or less of their basic needs. The convergence of conflict, disaster, and economic decline continues to erode
coping capacities, pushing Myanmar further toward a protracted humanitarian emergency with no signs of de-escalation.
5. International condemnation has intensified following the 10 December 2025 airstrike on Mrauk-U Hospital. The UN High
Commissioner for Human Rights called for an investigation, warning the attack could amount to a war crime. WHO's Director-General
condemned the strike as among dozens of verified attacks on healthcare in 2025. Amnesty International and the Burma Human Rights
Network have urged the UN Security Council to refer Myanmar to the International Criminal Court, impose an arms embargo, and
authorize emergency cross-border humanitarian aid.
Peace negotiations remain effectively stalled: resistance leaders and the National Unity Government publicly rejected
Chinese-brokered terms for northern Shan State. The junta cancelled voting in over 67 townships where it cannot secure control, while
nationwide "silent strikes" signalled popular rejection of the military's December 2025 elections. EU and Australia have declared the
vote "not credible" amid junta repression. The junta denied responsibility for civilian casualties, accusing "terrorists" of being targeted,
while humanitarian organizations stated that the pre-election environment has driven further escalation rather than de-escalation.
6. After taking office on 10 April 2026, president Min Aung Hlaing announced a 100-day program inviting resistance groups — both NCA
signatories and non-signatories, including People's Defense Force (PDF) units — to enter peace talks by 31 July 2026. However, the
Karen National Union (KNU), All Burma Student's Democratic Front (ABSDF), and the Chin National Front (CNF) quickly rejected the offer,
with the KNU stating it has no intention of negotiating under frameworks linked to military rule, underscoring the deep erosion of trust
between the junta and resistance forces.
5
Operational Environment
Economy
Current Economic Situation
Myanmar's bilateral trade with India was reported at approximately US$1.95–2.0 billion in 2025–2026, with both governments agreeing
to accelerate this toward short-term targets of US$3 billion and eventually US$5 billion [26][39][28][6]. Myanmar's leadership has
sought investment in agriculture, timber, minerals—including rare earths—rubber, information technology and digital infrastructure
[6][26]. To support trade, India and Myanmar agreed to facilitate bilateral transactions through a Rupee–Kyat settlement mechanism,
which has recorded steady growth since its operationalisation in May 2024 [26]. India signalled it will continue engagement with
Myanmar despite Western sanctions imposed after the 2021 coup, with Indian officials arguing sustained dialogue is preferable to
isolation [48][28].
Myanmar's extractive sector remains a major global supplier of rare earths, copper, tin and gemstones, with significant Chinese
investment and largely unregulated operations in conflict-affected areas, exposing the industry to operational and safety risks
[34][21]. The junta introduced measures to encourage electric-vehicle imports—including trade-in schemes—amid heavy energy
import dependence (approximately 90% of supply), while EV exemptions from alternate-day driving rules have pushed up prices and
created market uncertainty for dealers [20]. Reports used a reference exchange rate of $1 = 2,100 MMK as of mid-March 2026 for local
conversion estimates [2].
Conflict Economic Landscape
President Min Aung Hlaing's May 30–June 3, 2026 visit to India underscored trade and investment ambitions, though analysts warned
the visit is unlikely to generate significant new investment given ongoing insecurity and the fact that large areas remain outside
central military control, constraining investor access and project delivery [6][26]. Both governments agreed to deepen cooperation
through the Rupee–Kyat settlement mechanism and collaboration on agro-processing, petroleum, energy, and mining, as well as
connectivity projects including the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport project and the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral
Highway—both of which remain delayed by security challenges in Myanmar [26][6][28]. Central bank leadership was included in the
Myanmar delegation, suggesting coordination on monetary and trade matters at senior levels [26].
Governance and safety risks in the extractive sector were highlighted by a major explosives blast at a mining site in Namhkam, Shan
State on 2 June 2026, underscoring unregulated operations and links to Chinese investors and armed groups in resource areas [34].
Conflict-driven disruptions have cut trade routes and supply chains and undermined livelihoods across the country. In Arakan
(Rakhine) State, a strict blockade and transport restrictions have displaced some 600,000 people since renewed fighting, driving food
price inflation and severely limiting market access [15]. New displacements in Tanintharyi of over 5,000 since mid-May 2026 have
further compounded these pressures [8]. Inle Lake communities in southern Shan State remain unable to repair earthquake damage a
year on, amid sharp cost increases—carpenter wages up to 45,000 MMK/day, a basic stilt house costing approximately 5 million MMK,
and rice reaching 160,000 MMK per bag—alongside a severely depressed tourism sector [5].
Health and basic-service recovery remains highly uneven: health partners reported operating in only 106 of 227 prioritized townships
(47%) and covering just 35% of the 86 townships classified as severity level 4, with 78% of high-severity health townships located in
areas not under military control [12]. Overall, insecurity, fragmented territorial control, weak governance in resource sectors and
constrained humanitarian funding are limiting investment, infrastructure reconstruction, and the restoration of livelihoods across
conflict-affected parts of Myanmar [6][12][15].
Stability of Currency and Bank System
India and Myanmar agreed on June 1, 2026 to facilitate and enhance bilateral trade through a Rupee–Kyat settlement mechanism,
noting steady growth in transactions since its operationalisation in May 2024 [26]. Bilateral trade was reported at over US$2 billion in
2025–2026, underscoring the commercial rationale for closer currency settlement arrangements [28]. Central bank leadership was
included in the Myanmar delegation to India in late May/early June 2026, suggesting coordination on monetary and trade matters at
senior levels [26].
The junta's commerce ministry announced an electric vehicle (EV) import-for-surrendered-vehicle scheme on May 28, 2026, stating
that the central bank would supply required foreign currency for permits at an "appropriate" exchange rate, indicating direct central
bank involvement in the allocation of foreign exchange for policy-led imports [20]. An alternate-day driving rule introduced in March
2026, from which EVs were exempted, combined with demand pressures, contributed to sharp EV price increases, with some models
reportedly reaching "hundreds of millions of kyat," reflecting market volatility [20]. Myanmar's heavy dependence on imported
energy—approximately 90% of supply—was cited by authorities as a key driver for prioritising EV imports to reduce fuel reliance [20].
Reports used a mid-market exchange rate of $1 = 2,100 MMK as of 18 March 2026 for conversion estimates [2].
Employment
Conflict-driven displacement has severely constrained livelihoods and employment across Myanmar. More than 3,000 internally
displaced persons in southern Rakhine (Taungup, Thandwe and Gwa townships) face acute food insecurity and a near-total absence
of casual labour or income [15]. Intensified operations since mid-May 2026 displaced over 5,000 people in Tanintharyi, and around
12,000 people remained displaced in western Bago since April 2026, limiting access to employment and basic services [8].
Local labour market data indicate sharp variability in wages and conditions. In the Inle Lake area of southern Shan State, carpenter
daily wages rose to 45,000 MMK, while typical daily earnings were reported at approximately 8,000 MMK for women versus up to
150,000 MMK for men; declines in tourism, including widespread hotel closures, have further reduced local jobs [5].
6
Extractive and mining activities in conflict-affected areas operate largely informally under armed groups, generating revenue and
employment but posing severe safety risks, as illustrated by a gelignite storage explosion in Namhkam that killed dozens and injured
scores in late May/early June 2026 [25][34].
Attacks on health care have significantly weakened health-sector staffing and service coverage. Insecurity Insight recorded 1,929
incidents of violence against health care across Myanmar between 1 February 2021 and 12 May 2026, with at least 173 health workers
killed and 930 arrested; 73 attacks were recorded between 1 January and 31 May 2026, while WHO verified 38 attacks in the same
period [11][12]. Health partners reported providing services in only 106 of 227 prioritized townships (47%) as of Q1 2026 [12].
Politics
Governance Structures and Rule of Law
Myanmar's ruling junta continues to seek international recognition while consolidating power. Junta leader Min Aung Hlaing visited
India and met Prime Minister Narendra Modi on 3 June 2026 to discuss trade, security, border management, and connectivity projects
[98][116][109][96]. His delegation included prominent business figures and representatives from the Union of Myanmar Federation of
Chambers of Commerce and Industry, highlighting close ties between the military leadership and private-sector cronies that raise
transparency and anti-corruption concerns [98]. Bilateral talks covered cooperation on cybercrime and human trafficking, and Indian
officials noted joint efforts that rescued over 2,400 Indian nationals from scam centres in the past 18 months [109]. The April 2026
parliamentary election was widely denounced as a sham that consolidated military control, after which Min Aung Hlaing assumed a
civilian presidential role [102]. The National Unity Government (NUG) formally urged India to weigh the broader implications of
engaging the junta, warning that such engagement could normalise military rule [109].
Armed governance fragmentation is pronounced in Rakhine State, where the Arakan Army states it controls almost the entire territory
and reports that junta bombardments and airstrikes on civilian towns have increased, reflecting contested authority and weakened
law-enforcement integrity [114]. Civil society monitors report that human rights abuses have worsened under the junta-turned
administration, with intensified air and drone strikes on villages, schools, and religious buildings, alongside widespread arbitrary arrests
and repression [82]. Political prisoners have died in detention due to lack of adequate medical care, with two reported deaths on
22–23 May 2026 [82]. The junta has tightened information controls, revoking the publishing licences of three media outlets on 11 May
2026 and arresting more than 200 social media users during the election period, according to independent press monitors [82].
Political Freedoms and Recent Laws
Since the 2021 coup, civil society monitors report intensifying arbitrary arrests, airstrikes, and repression, with human rights groups
saying conditions have worsened rather than improved [82]. The Assistance Association for Political Prisoners (AAPP) reports the
regime currently holds more than 22,000 people on political charges, while nearly 9,000 have been released [106]. Local monitoring
groups recorded two political prisoner deaths in custody on 22 and 23 May 2026, highlighting detention-related medical neglect and
abuses [82].
A Myanmar Internet Project analysis released in late May documented 374 arrests for online expression — 114 of those arrested were
women — and describes systematic digital repression through shutdowns, surveillance, and weaponized laws that drive
self-censorship and increase physical risks for those seeking signals in remote areas [87]. Authorities reportedly tracked down and
arrested more than 200 social media users during the election period, further signaling an expanding crackdown on independent
media and online dissent [82].
Women's rights monitors documented a rise in gendered violence linked to the conflict, including 44 women killed in April amid air and
ground attacks by junta forces [82]. Sexual violence is being used as a documented tactic of political repression, forming part of a
patterned repertoire of abuses against civilians and detainees [97].
Min Aung Hlaing's state visit to India from 30 May–3 June 2026 and related bilateral agreements — including a Rupee–Kyat trade
settlement announced on 1 June — prompted criticism from Myanmar opposition figures and regional rights parliamentarians who
warned the engagement risks legitimising the junta [109][91][69]. Overall, authorities are applying digital restrictions, punitive arrests,
and administrative measures selectively to shrink civic space and inhibit political participation and independent journalism [87][82].
Influence of Non-State Actors and Political Factions
Since the 2021 coup, Myanmar's conflict has been highly fragmented, with numerous ethnic armed organisations exercising local
control and parallel administration across large swathes of the country [76][105][104]. Several groups, including the Karen National
Union, have treated pre-coup ceasefires as void, expanded territorial governance, and continue to press for a federal system,
deepening fragmentation and complicating centralised authority [105][104]. In Shan State, groups such as the TNLA control territory
and economic assets that fund and reinforce their local authority [129].
Both non-state armed groups and the Tatmadaw have increased their use of air power and armed drones, producing cross-border
incidents and civilian deaths — including drone explosions on the Thai border and deadly incidents on the Bangladesh border on 24
May and 2 June 2026 [119][76][82]. In Rakhine (Arakan) State, the Arakan Army claims control of almost the entire territory, while a
junta-imposed blockade and active fighting have contributed to roughly 600,000 people displaced since November 2023 and severe
restrictions on humanitarian access [114][95]. Conflict-related sexual violence by both state and non-state actors is documented as a
systematic tactic of political repression and intimidation [97].
Regional engagement with the military government — including high-level visits and security cooperation by neighbours such as India
— sustains informal external ties that affect the junta's legitimacy and governance calculus [96][112].
7
Public Trust in State Institutions
Multiple patterns of junta conduct have been documented by civil society and local monitoring groups, pointing to a marked erosion
of legitimacy and public confidence in state institutions. Civil society monitors report intensified junta violence — including daily
airstrikes, drone strikes, ground assaults, arbitrary arrests, and attacks on villages, schools, and religious buildings — alongside the
revocation of publishing licences by the Ministry of Information on 11 May 2026, indicating sustained repression of dissent and
information flows [82][87].
Local rights groups recorded extensive civilian property destruction and displacement in May: the Karenni Human Rights Group
reported more than 120 houses, vehicles, and other properties damaged in Karenni State, including around 106 buildings destroyed by
arson in Hpruso Township and roughly 140 households (approximately 7,000 people) forced to flee during operations that month [127].
A mortar explosion on 2 June killed a child near the Bangladesh–Myanmar border in Bandarban's Naikhongchhari area, highlighting
continued spillover insecurity from Myanmar's conflict [76]. These patterns — attacks on civilians and health services, digital
repression, media shutdowns, and mass property destruction — collectively underscore the deep erosion of institutional legitimacy
under the junta [82][87][127][123].
Role of Marginalized Groups
Marginalized communities — including women, ethnic minorities, and political detainees — face acute and compounding
vulnerabilities under the junta's ongoing military operations. The military conducts near-daily airstrikes and drone strikes targeting
villages, schools, and religious buildings, severely constraining the civic space of affected communities, particularly ethnic populations
in conflict-affected areas [82].
Violence against women and girls has risen sharply, with the Burmese Women's Union documenting 44 women killed in April alone
amid military operations [82]. Digital repression disproportionately affects women and activists: of the 374 people arrested for online
expression documented by the Myanmar Internet Project, 114 were women, while communications blackouts force people to travel long
distances to access signals, increasing physical risks [87]. Ethnic armed organisations, including the Karen National Union and groups
in Shan State, continue to exert territorial and political influence, with minority communities caught between competing armed actors
and the junta's forces [105][104][129]. Media suppression — including the revocation of publishing licences for multiple outlets in May —
has further shrunk avenues for marginalised groups and civil society to participate in public life [82].
Security And Stability
Security Overview
Military operations — including frequent airstrikes and drone strikes alongside large-scale ground offensives — have intensified across
multiple regions, causing increased civilian harm and displacement [148][183]. Since mid-May, operations in Tanintharyi Region
displaced more than 5,000 people sheltering in forested areas with severe shortages of food and basic supplies, and in western Bago
around 12,000 people remained displaced since April amid continued airstrikes and constrained humanitarian access [169]. A junta
offensive and accompanying aid blockade along the Chin–Magway border forced over 14,000 civilians to flee into mountainous areas,
where camp managers reported acute shortages of shelter, medical supplies and food and documented executions and other killings
during May operations [171]. Active frontlines, aerial bombardment and reported aid blockades continue to constrain humanitarian
access and elevate protection risks for civilians and aid workers [171][148][169].
Civil society groups on 2 June urged Japanese companies KDDI and Sumitomo to end partnerships with junta-linked Myanma Posts
and Telecommunications (MPT) over concerns that MPT's networks enable mass digital surveillance used by the junta to track and
repress civilians [172]. The junta leader's state visit to India (30 May–3 June) drew condemnation from ASEAN parliamentarians and
rights groups, who warned the visit risks legitimising the junta and underscored regional political tensions [173][162].
Security Forces and Law Enforcement
Intensified military operations, including airstrikes and drone attacks in Chin, Magway, Rakhine, Sagaing, Kachin, Karenni and northern
Shan, have severely impeded access to health care and the transport of medical supplies [138]. Between 1 January and 31 May 2026,
Insecurity Insight recorded 73 attacks on health care while WHO's Surveillance System for Attacks on Health Care verified 38 incidents,
with heavy weapons accounting for the largest share of incidents (approximately 70% in 2025 and 74% in the first five months of 2026),
indicating sustained use of heavy force against health infrastructure [145]. Since the 2021 coup, Insecurity Insight documented more
than 1,929 incidents of violence against health care up to 12 May 2026, with 66% of attacks attributed to the Myanmar Armed Forces, at
least 173 health workers killed, 930 arrested and health facilities damaged on at least 503 occasions [139]. Specific incidents recorded
in May 2026 include a 19 May landmine/ambulance attack that damaged an LNGO ambulance and killed an LNGO worker, and artillery
damage to two station hospital buildings in Mandalay on 24 May 2026 [134].
The Myanmar Health Cluster reports that health partners operated in 106 of 227 prioritized townships (47%) in Q1 2026, and that only 30
of 86 severity level 4 townships (35%) had partner interventions, with 78% of high-severity townships located in areas not under
Myanmar military control [145]. Ongoing registration restrictions imposed by de facto authorities, together with intensifying conflict, are
forcing some humanitarian partners to cease activities and are severely constraining service delivery and accessibility in rural and
high-severity areas outside urban centres [145].
Myanmar's leadership engaged externally in late May–early June 2026, with President Min Aung Hlaing meeting Indian leaders to
discuss border security and pledging that Myanmar territory would not be used against India's security interests, while India noted
cooperation on repatriating over 2,400 nationals from cyber-scam centres in Myanmar [136][141]. The junta's digital repression and
surveillance ecosystem has driven prosecutions and detentions for online activity, with documented arrests totalling 374 people, of
whom 114 were women in the reported period, further undermining civil liberties and enabling targeted enforcement actions [144][172].
8
Monitoring mechanisms also report that sexual violence is being used as a tactic of political violence in Myanmar, reflecting grave
protection concerns associated with security forces and other armed actors [166].
Demography
Demographic Overview
As of early June 2026, conflict-driven internal displacement is concentrated along the Chin–Magway border, where Mindat Township's
displaced population rose to about 17,000 — including roughly 7,000 evacuated from Mindat town, 7,000 from neighbouring villages,
and some 10,000 long-term IDPs — as of 2–3 June 2026 [190][189]. A regional snapshot for 26 May–1 June 2026 reported intensified
operations in Tanintharyi displacing more than 5,000 people since mid-May, and about 12,000 people remaining displaced in western
Bago since April, with humanitarian access constrained in those areas [191]. The humanitarian and health impacts of the conflict span
diverse ethnic areas — including Chin, Kachin, Karen/Kayin, Karenni, Mon, Rakhine, Sagaing, Shan and Tanintharyi — reflecting
multi-ethnic displacement and service gaps across both rural and border communities [184][193].
The Health Cluster reported that in Q1 2026, partners were providing health services in 106 of 227 townships prioritized in the 2026
Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (47%). Of 86 townships categorized as 'extremely deprived' (severity level 4), partners
reported interventions in only 30 (35%), noting that 78% of high-severity townships are located in areas not under Myanmar military
control, which limits access [184].
UNHCR reported approximately 1.2 million Rohingya refugees living in Bangladesh, including some 150,000 arrivals since early 2024 and
roughly 750,000 who fled during the August 2017 influx [212][201]. UNHCR and partners appealed for $710.5 million for the Rohingya
response, with the appeal around 60% funded at the time of reporting [201]. UN agencies noted that 2025 was the deadliest year on
record for maritime departures by Rohingya, with nearly 900 people reported dead or missing in the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal,
highlighting ongoing cross-border protection pressures [201][214]. UNHCR also reported in 2025 that more than 4.4 million people were
stateless globally, with Myanmar among the countries hosting large stateless populations, reinforcing the regional dimensions of
displacement and exclusion [211][212].
Socio-Cultural
Socio-Cultural Overview
Myanmar's social landscape is deeply fractured along ethnic, political, and geographic lines, with control contested between the
military and multiple ethnic armed organisations and local People's Defence Forces. Mawdaung town had been under Karen National
Union, Karen National Liberation Army, and People's Defence Force control for six months before being re-seized by the military on 19
May 2026 [258][232]. High-severity, health-deprived townships are disproportionately located in areas not under junta control—78% of
severity level-4 health townships fall outside military control—limiting partner access and services in those communities [230].
Intensified offensives have generated large internal displacements along ethnically mixed frontlines: roughly 14,000 people fled the
Chin–Magway border area in mid-May to early June 2026, including about 7,000 evacuees from Mindat town and 7,000 from
neighbouring villages, with junta blockades and the monsoon aggravating acute shortages of shelter, food, and medicine, and
widespread exposure to wet, moldy rations and inadequate roofing materials [226].
Rohingya camps and borderlands are reported to be embedded within wider conflict dynamics—armed recruitment, criminal
networks, and spillover insecurity affect camp and host-community social cohesion and protection [266]. Civilians and civic
institutions face targeted repression: junta operations include airstrikes and attacks on villages, schools, and religious buildings, and
several independent media licences were revoked on 11 May 2026 [231]. Violence against health services is pervasive and erodes
community resilience: Insecurity Insight recorded 1,929 incidents of violence against health care between 1 February 2021 and 12 May
2026, with 66% attributed to the Myanmar Armed Forces, at least 173 health workers killed, 930 arrested, and health facilities damaged
on at least 503 occasions [232]. The growing use of armed drones has both targeted medical services and produced cross-border
harm, including an errant drone blast that killed three Myanmar migrant workers in Thailand in early June 2026 [257]. Information and
digital environments are highly restrictive and polarised, shaping public narratives about aid, displacement, and accountability and
complicating humanitarian communication with affected communities [258]. Observers report that shared trauma from widespread
atrocities is fostering socio-political alignment between the Bamar majority and ethnic minorities, strengthening a collective
resistance identity that is reshaping communal relationships and claims to belonging [225].
Gender Dynamics
Civil-society monitoring indicates rising violence against women: the Burmese Women's Union documented 44 women killed in April
2026 from junta air and ground attacks, and reporting by Atrocity Alert and the UN notes that sexual violence in Myanmar is used as a
tool of political violence and collective punishment, increasing stigma and barriers for survivors to access protection and
survivor-centred services [231][261]. Between 1 January and 31 May 2026, Insecurity Insight recorded 73 attacks on health care and
WHO's Surveillance System for Attacks on Health Care verified 38 attacks in the same period [230][235]. Insecurity Insight has also
documented at least 53 maternal health services damaged, disrupted, or otherwise affected, reducing access to care for pregnant
women, mothers, and newborns [232]. On 1 June 2026, UNFPA reported organising two Clinical Management of Rape (CMR)
capacity-building sessions and, together with PATH, developing a 2026–2030 Family Planning Investment Case and conducting
family-planning awareness activities to address increasing reproductive health needs [230]. The Myanmar Internet Project found 114
women among 374 people arrested for online expression in its dataset and warned that internet shutdowns force women to travel to
remote locations to access signals, heightening risks of violence and gender-based discrimination [244].
9
Impact of Socio-Cultural Drivers on Aid
The junta's intensified digital repression—internet shutdowns, surveillance, and weaponised laws—has generated widespread anxiety,
prompted self-censorship, and forced people in areas such as Thandwe and parts of Rakhine to travel long distances to reconnect,
undermining safe and consistent communication channels for humanitarian engagement [244]. Insecurity Insight monitoring from
13–26 May 2026 shows contested social-media narratives and growing mistrust toward aid actors—with community expressions such
as "We Haven't Received A Single Bottle Of Water" and "The UN Shouldn't Even Exist Anymore"—signalling damaged community trust
and risks to the perceived neutrality and accountability of humanitarian messaging [258]. Sharp funding cuts and constrained access
for Rohingya refugees and host communities are leaving vulnerable groups—including women and girls, persons with disabilities, and
older people—highly dependent on aid and increasing tensions between host and displaced populations [260][264][267].
Cross-border incidents, including landmine explosions on 24 May and a deadly mortar on 2 June, reflect how borderlands have
become contested spaces controlled by multiple armed actors, eroding state governance and complicating humanitarian access,
local coordination, and acceptance of external responders [266]. Local socio-economic dynamics—such as gendered wage
disparities and repeated natural hazards in areas like Inle Lake that have forced households to prioritise daily survival over
rebuilding—alter informal support networks and influence how communities engage with and depend on humanitarian assistance
[286].
Environment
Environmental Conditions
Myanmar's 2026 monsoon had a late onset, leaving acute watery diarrhoea (AWD) cases lower than the same period in 2025 [319].
Hydrometeorological forecasts in early June 2026 warned of heavy thunderstorms and flood risk, with GLOFAS and Myanmar's
Department of Meteorology and Hydrology flagging Yangon and Bago states as particularly at risk, including scenarios up to
1-in-20-year flood events [320]. WMO seasonal outlooks indicate a pronounced shift toward El Niño for June–August 2026 (around 80%
probability), with the Maritime Continent expected drier-than-normal — a regional climate driver likely to influence Myanmar's
precipitation patterns and extreme-weather risk [320]. Parts of Myanmar experienced severe haze from land and forest fires in early
2026, peaking in March, contributing to transboundary air-quality challenges and increased respiratory risk for vulnerable populations
in the Mekong sub-region [303]. In Inle Lake (Nyaungshwe Township), the lake level rose by about three inches with the onset of the
rainy season and sediment accumulation at the lake bed is increasing local flood risk to plantations and settlements — compounded
by unrepaired damage from the 28 March 2025 earthquake [333]. Overcrowding in temporary settlements during the rainy season
was highlighted as increasing risk of skin and water-related diseases, reinforcing the need for WASH interventions [319].
Environmental Challenges
Localized AWD/cholera outbreaks were detected in Karen, Karenni, Mon, Sagaing and Southern Shan, driven by chronic poor hygiene
and contaminated drinking water [319]. Malaria surges were also reported in Chin, Kachin and Tanintharyi, driven by poor WASH
conditions, limited diagnostics and insufficient vector control [319]. Monsoon rains in May–June compounded humanitarian needs: a
junta offensive combined with torrential rains displaced roughly 14,000 people around Mindat in early June 2026, leaving displaced
families exposed and lacking shelter, food and medical supplies amid a junta blockade of supply routes since 14 May [289]. Intensified
fighting, heavy bombardments and airstrikes have damaged towns, driven displacement and contributed to broader environmental
degradation in conflict-affected areas, complicating access for environmental and WASH responses [338][341]. The Health Cluster
warned that conflict and access constraints — with most high-severity health townships outside junta control — combined with
transport bans (e.g., medicines blocked at Pakokku) and deliberate blockades are severely limiting preparedness, anticipatory action
and response capacity [319][300][289].
Environmental Risks and Mitigation
GLOFAS and NOAA/FEWSNET forecasts in June 2026 indicated up to 300 mm of rainfall in a 10-day period and a risk of up to
1-in-20-year flooding for Yangon and Bago states, while the Department of Meteorology forecast thunderstorms during the first 10
days of June — raising the risk of flash floods and landslides flagged by regional risk monitors and the Start Fund [320][317]. Inle Lake
communities face recurring seismic and hydrometeorological hazards, including repeated floods, droughts and windstorms, with
earthquake damage from March 2025 remaining largely unrepaired [333]. In response to these compounding risks, Health and WASH
partners have undertaken joint AWD action planning, developed a Township Prioritization Tool, and are expanding prepositioning of
medical supplies for rapid deployment to hard-to-reach areas [319][290]. UNICEF organized an AWD preparedness workshop in
Myitkyina on 4–5 June 2026, and updated AWD action plans have been developed for Northwest, Karenni, Shan, Rakhine and Southeast
regions [319][290].
Conflict
Overview of the Ongoing Armed Conflict
Since mid-May through early June 2026, active hostilities have been reported across multiple areas of Myanmar — notably northern
Shan (Namhkam), Rakhine (Kyaukphyu/Ramree), Chin (Mindat), Tanintharyi and western Bago — producing new displacement and
civilian harm [390][379][370][388][378][367][359]. A massive detonation of stored mining explosives in Namhkam (northern Shan)
around 31 May–1 June killed dozens (reports range from at least 39 up to 55), injured many and destroyed scores of homes, with
casualty and damage figures varying between sources [390][379][370][388][380]. Junta air and naval strikes and ground fighting
around Kyaukphyu intensified at end-May/early June, with airstrikes on 28 May and 1 June reported to have hit IDP shelter sites near
Mount Peinhne, killing and injuring civilians and forcing thousands from over 30 villages to flee into forested areas [378].
10
Fierce fighting and junta counter-operations in Chin State have driven large new displacement into Mindat Township, where local
actors estimated about 17,000 people displaced as of 2 June 2026 [367].
Conflict intensity is marked by frequent airstrikes and rising drone use, and attacks on health care are widespread. Insecurity Insight
recorded 1,929 incidents of violence against health care from 1 February 2021 to 12 May 2026, attributing 66% to the Myanmar Armed
Forces and documenting at least 173 health workers killed, 930 arrested, 503 health facilities damaged and more than 80
drone-related incidents affecting health services [352][346]. Specific May 2026 incidents include an LNGO ambulance damaged by a
landmine on 19 May that killed an NGO worker and injured others, hospitals and clinics being shelled or militarised, and destruction of
medical infrastructure undermining service delivery and disease surveillance [352].
Cross-border spillover risks have increased, including an errant combat drone that killed three Myanmar migrant workers in Thailand
and recurring stray-ordnance incidents affecting Bangladeshi border communities [401][386]. Humanitarian access remains severely
constrained by active hostilities, blockades and insecurity, and UNHCR and humanitarian partners have warned that funding cuts and
access constraints are worsening conditions for Rohingya refugees and newly displaced populations in Rakhine and other areas
[376][391][378][359].
Conflict Stakeholders
The Myanmar military (Tatmadaw/junta/State Security and Peace Commission) remains the principal state actor, conducting
intensified ground offensives and coordinated aerial bombardments since leadership changes in March–April 2026, pursuing
consolidation of territorial control and international re-engagement [409][405]. It increasingly relies on airpower, sieges, forced
conscripts and large-scale offensives to hold towns and supply routes, while its overall combat capability is gradually degrading
[369][352][409][356].
Ethnic armed organisations and resistance forces — notably the Ta'ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), Arakan Army (AA), Myanmar
National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), Kachin Independence Army (KIA), Karen National Union (KNU), and local People's Defence
Forces (PDF) aligned with the National Unity Government (NUG) — control contested territories and conduct sustained operations
against the junta using decentralized guerrilla tactics, drones and localized administration to erode junta supply lines
[395][379][357][402][389][369]. The TNLA, a member of the Three Brotherhood Alliance, controls parts of northern Shan State including
Namhkam and relies on mining revenues; an accidental detonation of stored gelignite in late May/early June 2026 highlighted the
risks of rebel-controlled, largely unregulated extractive operations [379][370][395]. The Arakan Army exerts de facto control over most
of Rakhine and has been generating diversified revenue for operations and services (e.g., a recently reported lottery) [379][399]. More
broadly, non-state armed groups and local militias use resource extraction, artisanal mining and trade networks to finance operations,
giving them significant economic leverage over territory and local populations [379][395]. Factional fragmentation, shifting local
alliances, and the economic importance of resource-rich borderlands sustain a fragmented battlefield in which non-state actors
wield substantial territorial governance and revenue-generation power [395][379][357].
China is an active external broker, having mediated ceasefires and exercising influence across parties, while India recently engaged
the junta at the highest level — hosting junta leader Min Aung Hlaing on a state visit in late May/early June 2026 — to deepen trade,
defence and border-security cooperation, reflecting competing regional external involvements [395][405][402]. The military's
entanglement with illicit economies and the role of Border Guard Forces and allied militias in facilitating cyber-scams and organised
criminal networks further amplify risks of transnational crime and prolonged instability [356].
Peace Negotiations
Mediation efforts remain fragmented and ad hoc, with no clear, sustained or inclusive negotiation process yielding a durable
settlement [347]. ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus remains the official regional framework but has delivered little progress since the 2021
coup, with limited implementation of its provisions and slow movement on the special-envoy process [347]. The Philippines' ASEAN
special envoy, Theresa Lazaro, visited Naypyitaw in early January, and Manila formally urged Myanmar on 6 May to allow the envoy to
meet detained leader Aung San Suu Kyi as part of broader engagement efforts [347]. India hosted junta leader Min Aung Hlaing and
reported that Suu Kyi's detention was raised "largely in the context of the peace process," with Indian officials stressing inclusion of all
stakeholders for an enduring peace [364]. Separately, Timor-Leste President José Ramos-Horta proposed convening the Tatmadaw,
ethnic armed organisations and the democratic opposition "under a tent," guided by a retired Southeast Asian four-star general, to
seek a humanitarian solution and allow unrestricted humanitarian access [347].
Conflict Outlook
A sustained negotiated settlement appears unlikely in the near term, with a protracted war of attrition more probable than rapid
de-escalation [356]. While the junta controls some major towns in Chin and Sagaing, its combat capability is degrading as it relies
increasingly on indiscriminate airstrikes and expendable infantry, while resistance forces continually sever military supply and support
lines [356]. The conflict has become a testing ground for drones, electronic warfare and low-cost decentralized combat tactics,
expanding the reach of hostilities and raising risks to civilians and humanitarian actors [350][351].
Cross-border spillovers are intensifying regional instability: violence, deaths and abductions along the Bangladesh–Myanmar frontier,
collapse of effective governance on the Myanmar side, and disrupted trade routes are straining bilateral relations and exposing
border communities to greater harm [386]. Humanitarian access is increasingly constrained by insecurity and new warfare tactics,
driving rising internal displacement, complicating Rohingya repatriation prospects, and leaving large numbers of border and internally
displaced populations exposed to severe protection and assistance gaps [386][354].

Displacement
Displacement Overview
Recent reports document multiple new and ongoing displacement events across Myanmar in late May–early June 2026, driven by
intensified military operations, airstrikes, and blockade tactics [447][440]. A major junta offensive launched in mid-May displaced
roughly 14,000 people who fled into forests and surrounding areas around Mindat town, with 7,000 evacuated from Mindat town and
around 7,000 from 13 villages in Saw Township joining approximately 10,000 long-term IDPs, bringing the township's total displaced
population to about 17,000 [448][438]. Clashes were reported to be ongoing into early June, with displaced families facing severe
monsoon exposure and acute shortages due to a junta-imposed blockade in place since 14 May [448][438]. Intensified operations
since mid-May also reportedly displaced more than 5,000 people in Tanintharyi Region, while western Bago Region has around 12,000
people displaced since April amid continued airstrikes and access constraints [453]. In southern Rakhine State, more than 3,000 IDPs
across Taungup, Thandwe, and Gwa townships face acute food insecurity and minimal humanitarian assistance [445]. Military
operations in Hpruso Township between March and May involved the burning of over 80 homes and forced villagers to flee into forests,
creating urgent shelter and food needs for newly displaced civilians [456].
Attacks on health care and the recurrent use of drones and heavy weapons have degraded health service access and are
compounding displacement risks and protection concerns across multiple states [440][447]. Health Cluster reporting highlights
overcrowding in temporary settlements, elevated risks of AWD/cholera and malaria during the monsoon, and ongoing AWD
preparedness and prepositioning actions in early June [441][447].
Living Conditions of the Displaced Population
Displaced families in Mindat Township are facing acute shortages of shelter, food, and medicine, exposed to torrential monsoon rains,
with reports of moldy rations, lack of tarpaulins, and a junta-imposed blockade disrupting transport of essential goods since mid-May
[448]. IDP camps in Karenni State have reported surges in malaria, dengue, respiratory illnesses, and skin diseases since the onset of
the rainy season, with the Interim Executive Council reporting 92,577 clinic visits and more than 10,000 malaria cases across four
camps; clinics face medicine shortages and some health teams visit camps only quarterly [421]. In southern Rakhine State, more than
3,000 IDPs sheltering in forested or mountainous areas and makeshift camps across Taungup, Thandwe, and Gwa townships face
acute food insecurity, rising food prices, increasing child begging, and a near-absence of humanitarian assistance ahead of the
monsoon [445]. Overcrowding and WASH gaps in temporary settlements are elevating disease risks, and Health and WASH clusters
have been updating AWD and measles preparedness plans while UNFPA prepositioned reproductive health kits to support service
continuity in late May–early June 2026 [441].
Violence against health care has been extensive and persistent: between 1 February 2021 and 12 May 2026 there were 1,929 recorded
attacks on health care (66% attributed to the Myanmar Armed Forces), with at least 173 health workers killed, 930 arrested, and health
facilities damaged on at least 503 occasions, further undermining displaced populations' access to care [440]. As of May 2026, health
services reached only 106 of 227 prioritized townships (47%) and 30 of 86 townships classified as extremely deprived of services (35%),
with intensified conflict, restricted NGO registration, and access constraints limiting service delivery in high-severity areas [441].
Drivers of Displacement
Conflict and political repression by the Myanmar military — including large-scale offensives, airstrikes, the "Four Cuts" strategy, and
deliberate blockades — are the primary drivers of displacement and severe access constraints for civilians and humanitarian actors
[438][448][429][441]. Junta-imposed blockades have cut transport of food, medicine, and essential supplies from Pakokku toward
western Yaw region townships since 14 May, aggravating shortages and humanitarian needs for displaced populations [448].
Monsoon rains and recurring natural hazards are compounding displacement impacts, with torrential rains worsening shelter, food,
and health conditions for those hiding in forests or informal sites [448][453]. Conflict-related sexual violence has also been
documented as part of the repertoire of political violence used in Myanmar, increasing protection risks for civilians [454].
Health service delivery is highly constrained by intensified clashes: partners reported providing services in 106 of 227 prioritized
townships (47%), with interventions submitted from only 30 of 86 townships categorized as severity level 4 (35%), and 78% of
high-severity health townships lying in areas not under military control [441].
Separately, targeted violence, persecution, and statelessness continue to drive Rohingya displacement. Roughly 150,000 new arrivals
fled renewed violence in Rakhine since early 2024, 2025 saw nearly 900 Rohingya reported missing or dead at sea, and prospects for
safe, voluntary return have faded [426][428][433]. These combined drivers — armed offensives, targeting and persecution,
access-denying blockades, seasonal hazards, and chronic displacement dynamics — are producing repeated and secondary
displacement, severely constraining humanitarian access and eroding prospects for safe return [448][441][426].
Integration
National and host-country policy constraints remain major institutional barriers to durable local integration for displaced populations.
Bangladesh maintains political limits on formal integration, and Malaysia is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention, while junta
restrictions and blockades inside Myanmar further foreclose options for safe return [418][450][472].
The wider Rakhine displacement since November 2023 totals some 600,000 people, and in southern Rakhine State more than 3,000
IDPs across Taungup, Thandwe, and Gwa townships face virtually no employment opportunities and inadequate shelter [445].
Inside Myanmar, intensified fighting around Mindat in early June 2026 has driven roughly 17,000 people into displacement, with
large-scale evacuations and acute shortages of shelter, food, and medicines compounded by a junta-imposed blockade and
ongoing monsoon conditions severely limiting any prospect of local stabilization or return [438][448].

Humanitarian Access
Humanitarian Access Overview
Health partners reported activity in 106 of 227 prioritized townships (47%) and interventions in only 30 of 86 'severity level 4' townships
(35%), with 78% of high-severity townships located outside Myanmar military control, which fundamentally limits access [485].
Intensified armed clashes and NGO registration difficulties imposed by de facto authorities are significantly reducing partners' access,
reporting capacity, and ability to operate in high-severity areas, with some partners forced to cease activities entirely due to
registration barriers, while persistent internet connectivity and data-management constraints further limit reporting [485]. Violence
against health care is widespread: Insecurity Insight recorded more than 1,929 incidents between 1 February 2021 and 12 May 2026 —
including at least 173 health workers killed, 930 arrested, 503 health facilities damaged, at least 53 maternal health services damaged
or disrupted, and over 80 incidents involving drones — with 66% of attacks attributed to the Myanmar Armed Forces [497][498]. Recent
operational risks include a 19 May 2026 landmine-damaged LNGO ambulance on the Leiktho–Toungoo highway that killed one LNGO
worker and injured others, and artillery damage to station hospital buildings in Natogyi township on 24 May 2026 [498]. Blockades and
supply-chain disruptions in Rakhine/Arakan have left many IDPs with minimal or no assistance and acute food insecurity in southern
Arakan townships where only a few aid groups operate [487][498]. Displacement and frontline advances continue to constrain
access, with Mindat Township displacement rising to around 17,000 as of 2 June 2026 amid junta counter-offensives, increasing urgent
needs and complicating humanitarian delivery [510]. In response, the Health Cluster is expanding prepositioning of medical supplies
for rapid deployment to hard-to-reach areas, and the WASH Cluster developed a Township Prioritization Tool to be tested in Kachin
during an AWD preparedness workshop on 4–5 June 2026, while AWD action plans are being updated for Northwest, Karenni and Shan,
Rakhine, and Southeast regions [485]. Sexual and reproductive health services are being delivered mainly through mobile and
community-based approaches, and UNFPA released 29 Inter-Agency Reproductive Health kits to partners to support CEmONC and
referral services [485].
Barriers to Humanitarian Access
Access constraints vary significantly by region. In southern Rakhine (Taungup, Thandwe, Gwa), severe shortages of assistance and
acute food insecurity affect over 3,000 IDPs, with junta-imposed blockades and a strict blockade in Arakan having severely disrupted
transportation and supplies since renewed fighting [487][479][498]. More than 14,000 civilians fled amid a junta offensive and aid
blockade along the Chin–Magway border, and multiple IDP camps in Karenni face clinic shortages and rising malaria and dengue risk
due to infrequent health visits and limited medical supplies [479][480]. Reported bans at military checkpoints on transporting
medicines and food from Pakokku further constrain humanitarian deliveries across affected areas [498].
Humanitarian Access Gaps
The most critical access gaps are concentrated among populations in high-severity townships, displacement sites, and refugee
communities where the combination of active hostilities, targeted attacks on health infrastructure, blocked routes, and funding
shortfalls prevents timely delivery of food, water, shelter, and health services [497][498][482][489]. Inside Myanmar, populations in
southern Rakhine townships, along the Chin–Magway border, and in Karenni IDP camps face the greatest difficulty accessing
humanitarian assistance due to the overlapping effects of insecurity, blockades, infrastructure damage, and insufficient partner
presence in areas outside military control [487][479][480][485]. Drone threats against health facilities represent an emerging and
growing operational gap, with over 80 such incidents already recorded, further restricting the ability of mobile and community-based
teams to safely reach underserved populations [497][498].
Information, Communication and AAP
Information Landscape
Information about Myanmar in early June 2026 is drawn from UN agencies, local monitoring groups, and open-source incident
trackers, producing partial overlaps and differing counts that require cross-validation for operational decision-making and response
prioritization [544][578][576]. Between 1 January and 31 May 2026, Insecurity Insight recorded 73 attacks on health care in Myanmar,
while WHO's Surveillance System for Attacks on Health Care (SSA) verified 38 attacks in the same period [544]. Analysis of incident
types shows heavy weapons caused 70% of verified attacks in 2025 and 74% during January–May 2026, indicating persistence of
high-intensity threats to health services [544]. Since the 2021 coup, Insecurity Insight has recorded 1,929 incidents targeting health
care, including at least 173 health workers killed, 930 arrested, and more than 503 health facilities damaged [535][534].
Community-based monitoring by KHRG, using trained local researchers reporting in March–April 2026, provides granular, redacted
incident narratives for human rights documentation and operational awareness, but censors names and precise locations for security
reasons [578][575][571]. Forecasting and anticipatory systems flagged heightened flood risk for Myanmar in early–mid June 2026, with
Start Network/Start Fund citing FEWSNET, NOAA, GLOFAS, and Myanmar's Department of Meteorology and Hydrology to encourage
anticipatory alerts and actions [551][562].
Communication Channels
Humanitarian actors and affected populations rely primarily on mobile/internet-based platforms, social media and other digital
platforms, and mobile- and community-based face-to-face approaches for information exchange [529][576][544]. Mobile networks
are highly compromised: civil society accuses the state-linked operator Myanma Posts and Telecommunications (MPT) of enabling
mass surveillance, censorship, and hosting junta propaganda sites, and companies linked to MPT were urged to divest in early June
2026 [529][526]. Internet shutdowns, pervasive surveillance, and frequent connectivity outages force people to travel long distances —
over 10 miles and multi-hour hikes in some areas — to find a signal, impeding remote reporting by partners and undermining
accessibility and reliability [526][544].
13
Digital platforms and social media are widely used for narratives around aid and displacement and are actively monitored by
organisations, but online expression is dangerous: large-scale arrests for online activity have been documented, and propaganda and
misinformation risks have been noted in monitoring briefs [576][526][529]. Face-to-face and community channels remain important
— most sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services are delivered via mobile and community-based approaches — but intensified
conflict and access constraints limit partner presence [544]. Health partners reported service delivery in only 106 of 227 prioritized
townships (47%), and just 30 of 86 'severity level 4' townships had partner intervention data in Q1 2026 [544]. Timeliness and accuracy
of information are further weakened by verification delays and restrictive information controls; the Health Cluster has highlighted
ongoing reporting challenges while planning SSA awareness sessions to increase direct reporting of attacks on health care
[576][535][544][534].
Barriers to Information
Access to information in Myanmar faces overlapping structural, security, and logistical barriers. The Myanmar Health Cluster reported
persistent internet connectivity problems and limited data-management capacity among partners in May–June 2026, undermining
timely reporting and information-sharing [544][534]. Ongoing issues with NGO registration by de facto authorities have forced some
partners to cease activities entirely, further restricting formal channels for public information and aid communication [544].
Additionally, bans on transporting medicines at military checkpoints compound access constraints alongside intensified armed
clashes [544][535][534].
Sustained violence against health services has created a climate of fear that hinders movement, reporting, and access to service
information. A 19 May 2026 incident on the Leiktho–Toungoo highway damaged an LNGO ambulance and killed a staff member,
illustrating how security incidents directly disrupt information flows and service delivery [576]. More than 80 drone-related incidents
have been recorded, reflecting an intensification of aerial threats [535]. Forecast heavy rains and flood risk in early June 2026 for
Yangon and Bago states are likely to create additional physical barriers to information access and aid delivery during the monsoon
period [551][562].
The Health Cluster is planning SSA awareness sessions and other measures to encourage reporting, but access constraints and
security risks continue to limit effective information dissemination [544][534].
Misinformation and Rumors
Within Myanmar-related humanitarian reporting, differences between open-source and verified data create additional verification
challenges: the Health Cluster noted 73 attacks on health care reported by Insecurity Insight between 1 January and 31 May 2026
versus 38 verified by WHO's SSA system, underscoring the risks of unverified reports shaping perceptions of health access and
response capacity [534][544]. To strengthen verification and trusted reporting, the Health Cluster planned SSA awareness sessions
starting 1 June 2026 to train and incentivize partners to report attacks on health care directly to the WHO SSA system [544].
Accountability Needs and Transparency
Accountability for the humanitarian response in Myanmar is constrained by significant coverage gaps and operational barriers. As of
Q1 2026, health partners reported providing services in 106 of 227 townships (47%) prioritized in the 2026 Humanitarian Needs and
Response Plan, and in only 30 of 86 townships categorized as severity level 4 (35%), reflecting major gaps in the highest-need areas
[544]. Constraints include intensified armed clashes, bans on transporting medicines at military checkpoints, NGO registration
requirements by de facto authorities that have forced some organizations to cease activities, and persistent internet and
data-management problems that limit partner reporting and community feedback [544][535][534].
The Health Cluster is taking steps to strengthen reporting and preparedness: conducting SSA awareness sessions to encourage
reporting of attacks, developing a Township Prioritization Tool, updating AWD Readiness Action Plans, expanding prepositioning of
medical supplies, and planning localization and risk-sharing workshops in mid-June to support partner reporting and risk mitigation
[544].
Legal and Policy
Legal and Policy Framework
The legal and policy environment governing the Myanmar crisis is shaped by both domestic repression and contested international
engagement. The junta's Ministry of Information revoked publishing licences for three media outlets on 11 May 2026, and restrictions on
digital freedoms continue to tighten under cybersecurity and election-related laws that civil society says have led to prosecutions of
hundreds of people [606][632]. Civil society organisations also publicly urged companies on 2 June 2026 to end partnerships with
state-linked telecom operator MPT over its role in enabling mass surveillance and censorship, framing this as a legal and
human-rights risk linked to corporate complicity in repression [632]. The junta-imposed blockade on Arakan (Rakhine) State since
November 2023 has severely disrupted transportation and supply chains, undermining livelihoods and sharply limiting humanitarian
access to displaced populations [612].
Key documented patterns of non-compliance with protections for health care include the following figures:
- 1,929 recorded incidents of violence against health care in Myanmar between 1 February 2021 and 12 May 2026, with 66%
attributed to the Myanmar Armed Forces [600][603][605].
- At least 173 health workers killed and 930 arrested [600][603][605].
- Health facilities damaged on at least 503 occasions and 80+ recorded drone incidents affecting health services
[600][603][605].
14
UNHCR data also place Myanmar among countries with large stateless populations in the Asia-Pacific, reinforcing chronic barriers to
legal identity, documentation and access to services for affected groups [611].
Regionally, Timor-Leste's president and others have urged renewed mediation under ASEAN mechanisms, noting the Five-Point
Consensus and debates over appointing an ASEAN-led mediator or special envoy to facilitate humanitarian access and dialogue
[618]. India hosted Myanmar junta leader Min Aung Hlaing on an official visit from 30 May–3 June 2026, a move condemned by ASEAN
Parliamentarians for Human Rights as legitimising the junta and flagged in a 28 May 2026 letter from the National Unity Government to
India's foreign minister [609][626][637].
Humanitarian Impact of Legislation
Legislation and administrative policies imposed by Myanmar's de facto authorities have created severe operational constraints for
humanitarian actors. NGO registration requirements and opaque accreditation processes have forced some organisations to cease
activities entirely [604]. As of May 2026, health partners were providing services in 106 of 227 prioritised townships (47%) and in only 30
of 86 townships rated severity level 4 (35%), a gap explained in part by the fact that 78% of the highest-severity health townships are
located in areas not under Myanmar military control, which reduces partner access and reporting capacity [604].
Direct obstructions to medical movements compound these barriers: junta checkpoints banned the transport of medicines from
Pakokku on 13 May 2026, and an LNGO ambulance hit a landmine on 19 May 2026 near Chauk Maing village (Leiktho township) —
despite having obtained junta clearance — killing one LNGO worker and injuring others, indicating ineffective or unreliable
safe-passage mechanisms [603][600]. Artillery shelling also damaged functioning hospital buildings on 24 May 2026 in Natogyi
township, further illustrating direct threats to humanitarian personnel, assets and facilities [600][603]. Between 1 January and 31 May
2026, Insecurity Insight recorded 73 attacks on health care while WHO's Surveillance System for Attacks on Health Care verified 38
attacks, signalling widespread violence undermining delivery of medical services across multiple states and regions [604][605][603].
Media and digital controls imposed by the de facto authorities — including revoking publishing licences in May 2026 and enforcing
cybersecurity and election-related laws — have driven arrests, internet shutdowns and pervasive surveillance, measures that impede
communications, reporting and protection for civilians and aid workers [606][608]. More broadly, sanctions, counterterrorism
measures and bureaucratic impediments are identified as drivers that further constrain humanitarian access, increase legal and
operational risks for aid actors, and hinder principled delivery of assistance [638].
International Agreements Impacting the Crisis
The international response to the Myanmar crisis is shaped by a combination of bilateral engagements, multilateral mechanisms and
targeted measures that have produced mixed results. ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus remains largely unimplemented since the 2021
coup, and regional mechanisms have struggled to progress meaningful mediation or ceasefire enforcement [618]. China has acted as
a regional broker, mediating a ceasefire with the Three Brotherhood Alliance in early 2024, underscoring Beijing's ongoing role in
conflict mediation dynamics [624].
India hosted Myanmar junta leader Min Aung Hlaing from 30 May–3 June 2026; Prime Minister Narendra Modi met him on 1 June and
both sides issued a joint statement to deepen cooperation, including facilitation of trade via a Rupee–Kyat settlement mechanism,
advancing connectivity projects, and increasing Mekong Ganga ICCR scholarships for Myanmar from 36 to 100 from 2026 onward
[627][626][633]. Indian officials stated that continued engagement aimed to support stability and was "not intended to be a
commentary on the internal political arrangements," arguing sustained dialogue is preferable to isolation [631][626][630]. The visit
drew sharp condemnation from ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights and multiple civil-society groups, who warned it risked
legitimising the junta [609][630][626][637].
Western targeted measures against Myanmar's senior leadership predate 2026: the United States first sanctioned Min Aung Hlaing in
2019, the UK imposed measures in July 2020, and the EU has maintained and extended sanctions. The Gambia's ICJ genocide case and
an Argentinian arrest warrant against Min Aung Hlaing were also reported in 2025 [639].
Global humanitarian funding shortfalls and donor cuts — including a reported 25% decline in total humanitarian funding in 2025 cited
by OCHA — are constraining international response capacity to the Myanmar-related displacement and refugee situations [645].
Limitations of Current Policies
Existing legal and policy frameworks exhibit significant gaps that undermine humanitarian response, human rights protection and
crisis resolution in Myanmar. Intensified conflict, daily airstrikes and growing drone use are severely impeding humanitarian access
and health service delivery, with health partners covering only 106 of 227 priority townships (47%) and just 30 of 86 extremely deprived
(severity level 4) townships (35%) as of early 2026 [604][605]. Administrative barriers imposed by de facto authorities — including
opaque accreditation requirements — have forced some partners to cease activities, creating bureaucratic impediments to
programme continuity and scale-up [604]. Safe-passage mechanisms have proven ineffective or unreliable, as demonstrated by the
medicine transport ban at Pakokku checkpoints on 13 May 2026 and the landmine incident on 19 May 2026 that killed an LNGO worker
despite prior junta clearance [603][600].
Information repression — including the revocation of publishing licences for three media outlets on 11 May 2026 and ongoing internet
restrictions — undermines transparency, monitoring and accountability for abuses and humanitarian needs [606][608]. The absence
of effective accountability mechanisms is further compounded by contradictory diplomatic moves: ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus
remains unimplemented, while India's hosting of coup leader Min Aung Hlaing during 30 May–3 June 2026 was condemned by ASEAN
Parliamentarians for Human Rights as legitimising the junta and inconsistent with democratic obligations [609][618].
15
Donor funding shortfalls are reducing operational scale and refugee support. A reported 25% decline in total humanitarian funding in
2025 cited by OCHA further narrows the space for principled, adequately resourced humanitarian action [645]. Collectively, these gaps
— spanning access constraints, impunity, information repression and financing shortfalls — point to the need for coordinated policy
reforms that strengthen humanitarian access guarantees, enforce existing international legal obligations, and sustain predictable
funding for crisis-affected populations.
