Sectoral Analysis
Food Security and Livelihoods
Access to Food and Market Functionality
Since mid-May, junta-imposed blockades and checkpoint restrictions have disrupted key supply routes and market access in western
and central Myanmar, including a ban on transporting medicines and food from Pakokku reported on 13 May and a broader cutoff of
transport toward western Yaw townships since 14 May [692][690][681]. Intensified fighting around Mindat and neighbouring areas
triggered large-scale displacement in early June — approximately 7,000 people evacuated Mindat town and a further 7,000 from
surrounding villages by 3 June, joining long-term IDPs and worsening local shortages as displaced families report moldy rations and
acute lack of essentials [681]. In southern Rakhine (Arakan), more than 3,000 IDPs face acute food insecurity driven by severe
shortages of humanitarian assistance, lack of income or casual labour, and sharply rising prices following a strict junta blockade that
has severely disrupted transportation and supply chains [677]. Local aid actors report extremely limited operational presence in parts
of southern Arakan — around three aid groups operating in some areas — and describe relief support as minimal to almost
nonexistent when it reaches displaced communities [677]. Since the renewed outbreak of conflict in Arakan (Rakhine) in November
2023, roughly 600,000 people have been displaced and the junta-imposed blockade has severely disrupted transportation and supply
chains, undermining local livelihoods and market access [677]. Commodity and basic food prices have climbed in conflict-affected
areas, eroding affordability for displaced and host households and prompting negative coping, while armed groups' economic
measures and blockades have been cited as drivers of higher living costs [677][700]. Intensified airstrikes, drone attacks and other
violence across Chin, Magway, Rakhine, Sagaing and other states are impeding movement of goods and humanitarian supplies,
constraining market functionality and limiting the ability of partners to replenish stocks or scale up distributions in high-severity areas
[675][674]. Start Network and seasonal outlooks flagged flood risk in Myanmar for June 2026, which may further disrupt markets,
transport routes and local food availability during the monsoon period [671].
Coping Mechanisms
Displaced households in southern Rakhine (Arakan) State face acute food shortages and minimal humanitarian support, with begging
increasingly used as a survival strategy and children reported among those begging in local markets [677]. Displaced families hiding
in the mountains along the Chin–Magway front have been reported eating moldy food rations and lack basic shelter materials such
as tarpaulins, heightening exposure and reducing food and non-food coping options [681]. IDP camps in Karenni State are dependent
on donor support for healthcare and nutrition, with medicine shortages, inadequate nutrition, and rising malaria and other disease
burdens undermining household resilience and coping capacity [691]. Overcrowding in temporary settlements and limited WASH and
medical supplies increase the risk of disease outbreaks, and AWD/cholera preparedness and WASH–health coordination activities —
including an AWD preparedness workshop planned for Kachin on 4–5 June 2026 — are underway to mitigate these risks [674].
Rohingya refugees from Myanmar remain heavily reliant on humanitarian assistance in Bangladesh, with funding cuts and food-ration
reductions deepening hardship and pushing some refugees to risky sea crossings; nearly 900 Rohingya were reported missing or killed
at sea in 2025, reflecting extreme coping-driven mobility and protection risks [665][676].
Livelihood Disruption
IDPs in southern Arakan State face near-total loss of income and virtually no casual day labour, with many resorting to begging and
lacking funds to buy shelter materials ahead of the monsoon [677]. In Karenni State, overcrowded IDP camps report rising infectious
disease caseloads and limited income, with clinics overstretched — 92,577 patients reported by the Interim Executive Council — and
families unable to afford transport or medicines [691]. Attacks on health care, including ambulance damage from a landmine and
bans on transporting medicines and food in areas such as Pakokku, have further disrupted service delivery and access to livelihoods
and essentials [690]. The Health Cluster reported ongoing NGO registration challenges and intensifying conflict that are impeding
health services, supplies and partner operations as of 1 June 2026 [674]. Agricultural livelihoods are being hit by deliberate military
actions, with reports of rice fields and other farming assets targeted, reducing farming income and food production capacity [701]. In
tourist-dependent Inle Lake (Nyaungshwe, southern Shan State), earthquake damage from 28 March 2025, high repair costs and
closed hotels have reduced tourism income while local costs and wages have shifted — carpenter wages up to 45,000 MMK/day,
women's casual wages around 8,000 MMK/day, and a bag of rice up to 160,000 MMK — eroding household purchasing power [666].
UNHCR and UN partners warned that Rohingya refugees remain largely dependent on aid with limited opportunities to earn, and that
funding shortfalls and restricted access are worsening livelihoods for refugees and host communities [665][676].
Impact on Agricultural Activities and Production
Military operations, airstrikes and ground fighting have driven displacement and acute shortages, disrupting rural livelihoods across
multiple regions of Myanmar [686]. Key displacement figures reflecting the scale of agricultural disruption include more than 5,000
people displaced from several villages in Tanintharyi Region since mid-May 2026, many sheltering in forested areas and facing severe
shortages of food and basic supplies, and around 12,000 people remaining displaced in western Bago Region since April 2026 amid
continued airstrikes and constrained humanitarian access [686]. Blockades, transport disruptions and constrained humanitarian
access have limited farmers' and traders' ability to reach fields and markets, reduced incomes from casual agricultural labour, and
contributed to soaring food prices and shortages of basic agricultural goods in affected areas [677]. Regionally, rising fuel costs and
global fertiliser shocks are increasing production and transport costs; World Vision notes El Niño and energy/fertiliser pressures across
mainland Southeast Asia, including Myanmar, are reducing input use and weakening fish and agricultural livelihoods [663]. Petrol
price spikes reported in regional coverage have exceeded 90% in the early months of the 2026 energy shock, further raising costs for
farm mechanisation, irrigation and transport and likely constraining input access [680][663].
Severe haze and fires that peaked in March 2026 across parts of the Mekong sub-region — including areas of Myanmar — have also
damaged agricultural areas and disrupted outdoor farming and fishing activities, compounding risks to upcoming planting and

harvest cycles [694].
Food and Livelihood Needs and Current Response
WFP restructured the Rohingya food response on 1 April 2026 by introducing a food insecurity-based Targeting and Prioritization
Exercise (TPE) that adjusted monthly entitlements while maintaining assistance coverage for all households, supporting 1.13 million
refugees in Cox's Bazar and 28,000 in Bhasan Char in April 2026 through general food assistance [660]. At TPE rollout WFP faced initial
beneficiary dissatisfaction and a temporary drop in collection rates, but full coverage was restored by mid-April through coordination
with UNHCR, authorities and community leaders [660]. In April 2026, WFP delivered nutrition services reaching 95,500 children (6–59
months) and 43,700 pregnant and breastfeeding women, and enrolled 4,710 children with moderate acute malnutrition into treatment
programmes [660]. The UN and the Government of Bangladesh launched a $710.5 million appeal for Rohingya refugees and host
communities for 2026 — 26% lower than the previous year and currently around 60% funded — raising concerns that funding shortfalls
will force hyper-prioritisation and reduce essential services [665][669]. Inside Myanmar, access constraints and limited relief have left
many displaced populations facing acute food insecurity, with reports citing over 14,000 civilians displaced toward the Chin–Magway
border with accounts of moldy food rations, more than 5,000 displaced in Tanintharyi since mid-May, and around 12,000 remaining
displaced in western Bago since April, all reporting severe shortages of food and basic supplies [677][681][686]. Blockades, disrupted
supply chains and frequent attacks on health services are undermining delivery of food, nutrition and livelihood assistance across
conflict-affected areas, further restricting humanitarian access and preparedness [677][690]. Health and WASH clusters are scaling
preparedness for monsoon risks by developing a Township Prioritization Tool, updating AWD/cholera action plans, expanding
prepositioning of medical supplies, and UNFPA released 29 Inter-Agency Reproductive Health kits while SRH services continue via
mobile and community-based approaches to reach underserved populations [674]. Coverage gaps remain significant: partners
reported health services in only 106 of 227 prioritized townships (47%), and only 30 of 86 townships rated as 'extremely deprived'
submitted intervention data, indicating major geographic and service shortfalls for life-saving health, nutrition and WASH interventions
that underpin food security and livelihoods [674]. Persistent funding shortfalls and access constraints continue to limit the scale and
effectiveness of food and livelihood assistance despite coordination efforts among WFP, UNHCR, local authorities and cluster partners
[660][665][674].
Education
Learning Environment and Facility Conditions
Following the reseizure of Mawdaung town by the Myanmar military on 19 May 2026, bunkers were observed at schools and station
hospitals, indicating direct militarization of education infrastructure [727][730]. More broadly, the Myanmar military has been reported
to target villages, schools, and religious buildings with airstrikes and drone attacks occurring almost daily in some areas, creating
acute safety risks for school premises and staff [750]. A Civil Disobedience Movement teacher was reportedly executed during
operations in Saw Township (Tapyin Village) in May 2026, illustrating direct threats to education personnel [749]. Data on violence
against civilian services record 1,929 incidents against health care between 1 February 2021 and 12 May 2026, reflecting the sustained
pattern of attacks that undermines civilian services including learning environments [730]. Intensified military operations and airstrikes
have driven large-scale displacement — more than 5,000 people in Tanintharyi since midMay 2026 and around 12,000 in western
Bago since April — with humanitarian access constrained in these areas [734]. Displaced families are sheltering in forested and
mountainous areas amid acute shortages of tarpaulins, shelter materials, and medical supplies, conditions under which schooling is
severely disrupted [749].
Access to Education and Barriers
Intensified military operations since midMay 2026 have driven new displacement that is directly constraining children's access to
school, with more than 5,000 people displaced in Tanintharyi Region and around 12,000 remaining displaced in western Bago Region
since April, and humanitarian access limited in both areas [734]. Overcrowding in temporary settlements and IDP camps, coupled with
rising infectious disease risk and shortages of services and transport, is further limiting children's ability to attend school [726][742]. In
southern Rakhine (Arakan), more than 3,000 IDPs across Taungup, Thandwe, and Gwa townships face severe shortages of assistance
and livelihoods, and reports of displaced children increasingly begging point to disrupted schooling and serious child protection
concerns [746]. Outside Myanmar, Rohingya refugees originating from Rakhine face persistent barriers to education and remain
heavily reliant on aid, with UNHCR and partners warning that a $710.5 million appeal that is only approximately 60% funded risks further
reductions in education and other essential services for this population [729][731].
Education Needs and Current Response
Across conflict-affected areas of Myanmar, children require expanded access to safe learning spaces, trained teachers, adequate
learning materials, and psychosocial support. Intensifying conflict and administrative obstacles — including NGO registration
impediments and constrained partner access in many highseverity townships — are limiting humanitarian presence and the ability of
organizations to deliver education and other services where they are most needed [726]. For Rohingya children from Myanmar in
Bangladesh camps, UNHCR and partners report education gains since 2017 but warn that sharp funding cuts now threaten these
services; the 2026 appeal for Rohingya refugees and host communities totals US$710.5 million and was reported at roughly 60%
funded, putting education, protection, and other services at risk [729][731]. WFP and other UN partners continue multisectoral
assistance in Cox's Bazar and report coordinated adjustments to aid delivery, while noting that education services remain vulnerable
to funding shortfalls and operational constraints [733][731].

Health
Availability and Access to Healthcare Services
Attacks on health care have been widespread and sustained, with 1,929 incidents of violence against health care recorded between 1
February 2021 and 12 May 2026; 66% attributed to the Myanmar Armed Forces; at least 173 health workers killed and 930 arrested;
health facilities damaged on at least 503 occasions; at least 53 maternal health services affected; and more than 80 incidents
involving drones [771]. Between 1 January and 31 May 2026, Insecurity Insight reported 73 incidents while WHO's SSA verified 38, with
intensified airstrikes and drone use across Chin, Magway, Rakhine, Sagaing, Kachin, Karenni and northern Shan severely impeding
access to care and medical supply transport [768]. An LNGO ambulance struck a landmine on 19 May 2026, killing one LNGO worker
and injuring other staff and patients, illustrating the high security risks for health actors and patients in transit [770].
Health partners operated in only 106 of 227 prioritized townships (47%) during Q1 2026 and submitted interventions from just 30 of 86
townships classified as severity level 4 (35%), with limited access to the highest-need areas largely because 78% of level-4 townships
are outside junta control and intensified clashes are impeding partner access and reporting [769]. Operational constraints include
NGO registration problems forcing some actors to cease activities, conflict blocking transport of medical supplies, and poor internet
and data-management capacity affecting reporting [769].
Recent hostilities and blockades are further disrupting medical supply chains: a junta-imposed blockade since 14 May has cut
transport of essential goods, food and medicine from Pakokku toward western Yaw townships, and an offensive along the
Chin–Magway border displaced roughly 14,000 people in early June, leaving displaced populations with acute shortages of medical
supplies [789]. In Karenni State IDP camps, access barriers are particularly acute — travel times to the nearest health centre are
approximately two hours, mobile health teams visit some camps only once every three months, and more than 10,000 people across
four camps have been affected by malaria alongside widespread respiratory and skin diseases and severe medicine shortages [772].
Disease Outbreaks
Since late May–early June 2026, Myanmar has reported localized outbreaks of acute watery diarrhoea (AWD), malaria, dengue,
mumps and persistent skin infections concentrated in conflict-affected areas and overcrowded IDP sites, driven by poor WASH,
displacement, limited diagnostics and constrained access to health services [769][768][772].
AWD outbreaks have been reported in Karen, Karenni, Mon, Sagaing and Southern Shan; while rapid detection and response contained
some cases early, limited rapid diagnostic tests, low risk awareness and chronically poor-quality drinking water sustain recurrence risk
[769][768]. Malaria surges attributed to lack of vector control and bednets were specifically noted in Chin, Kachin and Tanintharyi, with
inadequate testing and treatment enabling rapid expansion [768]. IDP camps in Karenni State reported simultaneous disease burdens
at the onset of the rainy season, including more than 10,000 people across four camps with increased malaria, widespread respiratory
illnesses, rising mumps among children since mid-May, and persistent skin disease, with clinics under-resourced and health teams
visiting infrequently [772]. Heavy rainfall forecasts for early June are elevating the risk of waterborne disease and flooding, increasing
AWD/cholera risk during monsoon onset [791].
Preparedness and response actions include subnational AWD Action Plan updates, expanded prepositioning of medical supplies by
the Health Cluster, and a UNICEF-supported AWD preparedness workshop in Kachin on 4–5 June 2026, alongside intensified measles
preparedness and health worker training in border areas at high risk from large outbreaks in neighbouring Bangladesh
[769][768][791].
Health System Challenges
Attacks on health care have critically undermined health system functioning across Myanmar. Between 1 February 2021 and 12 May
2026, Insecurity Insight recorded 1,929 incidents of violence against health care, with 66% attributed to the Myanmar Armed Forces, at
least 173 health workers killed, 930 arrested, and health facilities damaged on at least 503 occasions [770][771]. Intensifying airstrikes
and drone use across Chin, Magway, Rakhine, Sagaing, Kachin, Karenni and northern Shan are severely impeding both access to care
and the transport of medical supplies [768].
Conflict-related access restrictions and blockades have further disrupted medical supply chains, with junta checkpoints banning
transport of medicines from Pakokku on 13 May 2026 and a subsequent blockade since 14 May cutting off essential goods to western
Yaw/Mindat, leaving displaced populations with acute medicine shortages and limited healthcare access [770][789]. Health service
coverage remains critically low: in Q1 2026, health partners provided services in 106 of 227 prioritized townships (47%) and submitted
interventions from only 30 of 86 "extremely deprived" townships (35%), with 78% of high-severity townships located outside junta
control [769].
Systemic humanitarian constraints compound these challenges, including NGO registration impediments with de facto authorities,
funding and reporting difficulties, and limited partner access. The ongoing conflict has also driven disease escalation, with malaria
surges in Chin, Kachin and Tanintharyi due to lack of vector control and bednets, and AWD outbreaks in Karen, Karenni, Mon, Sagaing
and Southern Shan, while Karenni IDP camps report rising malaria, dengue, respiratory and skin diseases with medicines in very short
supply [768][772].
Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS)
The sustained campaign of violence against health care in Myanmar has severely undermined access to mental health and
psychosocial services. The widespread attacks on health facilities and workers — including 930 health workers arrested and 503
occasions of facility damage since February 2021 — have reduced the overall health system capacity within which MHPSS services
would ordinarily be delivered, with health partners reaching only 47% of prioritized townships as of Q1 2026 [770][771][769][768].
19
Community and civil society initiatives provide targeted psychosocial support in this constrained environment. The Assistance
Association for Political Prisoners (AAPP) offers psychological support, online mental health training and psychological training for
recently released political prisoners to reduce stigma and link them to professional services, while the ICRC assists by covering travel
costs that help maintain prison–family contact and support mental well-being [786]. Digital repression, internet shutdowns and
surveillance are reported to cause widespread anxiety and self-censorship, increasing psychosocial stress among civilians and raising
protection risks for women's rights defenders and other activists [795]. UN reporting and atrocity monitoring note a sharp rise in
conflict-related sexual violence in 2025, documenting its use as a tactic of political violence, and indicating increased need for
survivor-centred MHPSS and funded survivor assistance [809].
Health Needs and Current Response
The most urgent health needs in Myanmar are concentrated among conflict-affected and displaced populations, particularly at the
onset of the 2026 rainy season. Communicable disease threats include malaria surges in Chin, Kachin and Tanintharyi, AWD/cholera
outbreaks in Karen, Karenni, Mon, Sagaing and Southern Shan, and rising skin infections, dengue risk and mumps among IDPs in
Karenni [768][769][772]. In IDP settings, coverage is particularly weak: Karenni camps report clinic visits only once every three months,
frequent medicine stockouts, and malaria outbreaks affecting tens of thousands across multiple camps, with roughly eight in ten clinic
attendees showing malaria symptoms in some locations [772].
Critical gaps include shortages of diagnostics and medicines, lack of vector control and bednets, inadequate WASH driving recurrent
AWD, insufficient prepositioned medical supplies for hard-to-reach areas, and partner constraints from NGO registration hurdles,
internet and data limitations, and intensified clashes restricting access and reporting [769][768][772][789]. Sexual and reproductive
health services are being delivered primarily through mobile and community-based modalities, with UNFPA releasing 29 Inter-Agency
Reproductive Health kits to support CEmONC services [769].
Ongoing and planned responses include the Health Cluster's expansion of prepositioning of medical supplies to strategic
hard-to-reach locations, initiation of Phase II of the Health Facility Survey, joint Health–Nutrition–WASH AWD action planning, a
UNICEF-supported AWD preparedness workshop in Kachin on 4–5 June 2026, intensified measles preparedness in Rakhine, a UNFPA
Pharmacist Working Group market assessment for medical suppliers, and upcoming NCD and localization workshops in June 2026 to
strengthen partner preparedness and risk mitigation [769].
Nutrition
Availability and Access to Nutrition Services
Health partners reported providing services in 106 of 227 townships (47%) prioritized in the 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response
Plan, while only 30 of 86 townships categorized as 'extremely deprived' submitted data on partner interventions (35%) [813]. Key and
sustained barriers to nutrition service delivery include widespread attacks on health care and access constraints: Insecurity Insight
recorded more than 1,929 incidents of violence against health care between 1 February 2021 and 12 May 2026, with 66% attributed to the
Myanmar Armed Forces, at least 173 health workers killed and 930 arrested, health facilities damaged on at least 503 occasions, and at
least 53 maternal health services damaged, disrupted, or otherwise affected by violence, including more than 80 recorded
drone-related incidents affecting health workers, facilities, transport, and service provision [816][819]. Intensified airstrikes and drone
attacks in Chin, Magway, Rakhine, and Sagaing are impeding access to health care and the transport of medical and nutrition
supplies, while junta checkpoints have at times banned the movement of medicines and food — further restricting supply chains
[811][816]. Administrative constraints — including NGO registration issues imposed by de facto authorities — and escalating fighting are
forcing some partners to cease activities and limiting access to high-severity townships [813].
Displaced populations face acute food and nutrition gaps: more than 3,000 IDPs in Taungup, Thandwe, and Gwa townships (southern
Rakhine) face severe food shortages and minimal humanitarian support, with children increasingly resorting to begging for food [814],
and renewed conflict in Arakan since November 2023 has contributed to roughly 600,000 people displaced and to prolonged
blockades that undermine supply chains and livelihoods [814]. In eastern and border IDP sites, nutrition and related health services are
extremely limited: several Karenni camps lack on-site clinics, health teams visit only once every three months, medicines and nutrition
support are in very short supply, and malaria outbreaks have affected over 10,000 people across four camps with around eight in ten
clinic patients showing malaria symptoms — all of which reduce the capacity for malnutrition prevention and treatment [818].
Joint Health–Nutrition–WASH preparedness actions are ongoing, including AWD risk indexing, AWD Action Plans, and prepositioning of
medical supplies for rapid outbreak response; UNICEF supported AWD preparedness training in Kachin on 4–5 June 2026, indicating
some coordinated preparedness efforts despite access constraints [811][813]. UNFPA released 29 Inter-Agency Reproductive Health
(IARH) kits to SRH partners to support service delivery, including referral hospitals providing Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and
Newborn Care (CEmONC) services [813].
Nutrition Needs and Current Response
Health and nutrition actors report active preparedness and targeted nutrition delivery amid severe access constraints and disease
outbreaks, but coverage gaps remain large [811][813]. WFP delivered nutrition services in April 2026 reaching 95,500 children (6–59
months) and 43,700 pregnant and breastfeeding women, and enrolled 4,710 children with moderate acute malnutrition in treatment
programmes for Rohingya refugees [812]. Humanitarian coordination has prioritized joint Health–Nutrition–WASH AWD preparedness —
including an AWD risk index, sub-national action plans, measles preparedness in Rakhine and Chin, health worker training, and
expanded prepositioning of medical supplies for rapid outbreak response [811][813].
Intensified airstrikes, drone attacks, and other insecurity continue to impede access for health and nutrition teams and the transport of
supplies, reducing treatment and prevention coverage [811].

Vector control gaps, lack of bednets, and shortages of medicines are driving malaria surges reported in Chin, Kachin, and Tanintharyi,
complicating nutrition-sensitive disease prevention in IDP settings [811][818]. Beyond southern Rakhine, recent displacements in
Tanintharyi (5,000+ since mid-May) and western Bago (approximately 12,000 since April) have been accompanied by reported

WASH
Availability of Water Sources
AWD outbreaks were detected in high-risk areas—Karen, Karenni, Mon, Sagaing, and Southern Shan—driven by chronic lack of hygiene
and poor-quality drinking water, though a late monsoon onset kept case numbers lower than in 2025 [843][844]. Overcrowding in
temporary and IDP settlements is a persistent driver of rapid AWD and skin disease spread as the rainy season begins, with limited
WASH services and medical supplies in many camps [843][850]. Forecasting products flagged heavy rainfall and flood risk in early
June 2026—including up to ~300 mm in 10 days and potential 1-in-20-year flooding affecting Yangon and Bago—heightening the risk
of water-supply disruptions and waterborne disease spread during the monsoon [867]. UN agencies warned that blocked
humanitarian access and funding shortfalls are leaving communities, including Rohingya refugees and newly displaced people,
without reliable access to clean water and basic WASH services [868][860].
Access to Sanitation Facilities and Hygiene Practices
IDP camps in Karenni State report poor WASH conditions, medicine shortages, lack of nearby clinics, and urgent needs for mosquito
nets as malaria and dengue surge alongside skin and respiratory infections [850]. Lack of vector control and insufficient bednet
coverage are driving malaria increases in Chin, Kachin, and Tanintharyi, exacerbating WASH-related health risks [844]. Joint
Health–Nutrition–WASH AWD action planning is underway at sub-national level as part of monsoon preparedness efforts, with limited
rapid diagnostics and community awareness identified as key barriers to outbreak control [844][843]. Mass displacement around
Mindat amid monsoon rains has left displaced populations exposed, with acute shortages of shelter, tarpaulins, food, and medical
supplies, heightening hygiene and disease-transmission risks in affected sites [875].
Waste Management and Vector-Borne Disease Risks
Intensified conflict and access constraints are significantly reducing health partner presence and reporting in high-severity townships,
limiting delivery of WASH and disease-prevention interventions [843]. Health partners active in only 106 of 227 prioritized townships
(47%) and reporting interventions from only 30 of 86 severity level-4 townships indicate major coverage gaps that also affect waste
management and vector control services [843]. A June risk bulletin warned of heavy mid-June rainfall and flooding risk, with Yangon
and Bago states particularly exposed—conditions that could worsen water contamination and increase vector proliferation risks [867].
The Health Cluster identified chronic poor hygiene and unsafe drinking water, limited rapid diagnostic tests, and low community
awareness as root causes enabling recurrent AWD outbreaks, and is updating sub-national AWD Readiness Action Plans alongside a
multisectoral Health-WASH-Nutrition AWD Risk Index [843].
Main WASH Needs and Humanitarian Response
Key WASH needs identified include chronic lack of hygiene, poor-quality drinking water, inadequate sanitation in overcrowded
temporary settlements, and limited rapid diagnostic testing and community awareness for AWD prevention [843]. Vector-control gaps
and shortages of bednets are driving malaria surges in Chin, Kachin, and Tanintharyi, increasing WASH-adjacent needs in IDP and
camp settings [844][850]. WASH Cluster preparedness and response measures include a Township Prioritization Tool for joint
Health–Nutrition–WASH planning, updates to AWD Action Plans for Northwest, Karenni and Shan, Rakhine, and Southeast, and an AWD
preparedness workshop in Kachin (Myitkyina) on 4–5 June 2026 organized by UNICEF [843]. Health and cluster partners are expanding
prepositioning of medical and outbreak-response supplies to strategic, hard-to-reach locations to enable rapid deployment during
AWD events [843]. Major constraints to scaling the WASH response include intensified armed clashes, airstrikes and drone attacks
restricting access, NGO registration barriers, transport bans at checkpoints, and persistent connectivity and reporting limitations
among partners [843][844][859].
Shelter and Non-Food Items (NFI)
Damage to Housing and Shelter Needs
Intense military operations and large explosions have caused widespread housing destruction and acute shelter needs across
multiple states in early June 2026 [898][926][912]. In Mindat (Chin–Magway border), roughly 7,000 residents evacuated Mindat town
and a further ~7,000 from 13 neighbouring villages since operations began on 13 May, joining some 10,000 long-term IDPs — putting
Mindat township displacement at an estimated ~17,000 people; displaced families are sheltering in forests and mountains and face
urgent shortages of tarpaulins, shelter, food and medical supplies ahead of the monsoon [898]. In Karenni State (May 2026), more
than 120 civilian properties were recorded damaged, including 96 houses (with 85 houses and 16 vehicles destroyed by fire), plus
damage to a school, a religious building and public-use facilities [903]. In Hpruso Township, over 80 homes were reported burned
across three villages between March and May (16 houses on 28 March; >60 houses on 6 May; 4 houses on 7 May), with displaced
civilians identified as needing shelter and food assistance [935]. In Northern Shan (Namhkam blast, 31 May), a massive explosion
levelled much of a village — reports describe more than 100 houses near the blast damaged, with accounts that "over half" of the
village's houses were destroyed [926][912][932].
21
In southern Rakhine/Arakan, some 3,000+ IDPs in Taungup, Thandwe and Gwa townships are sheltering in forested or mountain areas
or makeshift camps and lack basic roofing and tarpaulins, leaving them exposed ahead of the monsoon [897]. Rebuilding and shelter
response are further constrained by high repair costs and scarce construction labour and materials — for example, Inle Lake
earthquake-damaged homes from 28 March 2025 remain unrepaired due to rising wages and material prices — as well as deliberate
destruction of communal infrastructure such as schools and public buildings in conflict-affected areas, compounding obstacles to
recovery and safe return [899][903].
Living Conditions in Camps or Settlements
Displaced populations across multiple regions face severe living conditions. Intensified operations since mid-May in Tanintharyi
displaced more than 5,000 people sheltering in forested areas with severe shortages of food and basic supplies, while western Bago
has around 12,000 people displaced since April with constrained humanitarian access and high needs for food, shelter and healthcare
[906]. Overcrowding in temporary settlements is driving disease spread: Karenni State camps report surges in malaria, dengue,
respiratory and skin infections with mumps rising among children since the second week of May, over 10,000 people across four camps
in eastern Loikaw Township affected by malaria, and some camps (e.g., Kyaytone) sheltering more than 200 households (2,000+
people) with no clinic inside and health teams visiting only quarterly [902]. The Interim Executive Council of Karenni State reported
92,577 patients visited clinics it operates, and health workers expect patient numbers to rise with the rainy season [902]. The Health
Cluster warned that overcrowding in temporary settlements heightens skin-disease transmission, that lack of vector control and
bednets is triggering malaria surges in Chin, Kachin and Tanintharyi, and that recurrent AWD/cholera outbreaks are linked to poor
hygiene and unsafe drinking water; health partners reported service delivery in 106 of 227 prioritized townships (47%) and in 30 of 86
townships classified as 'extremely deprived' (35%), reflecting limited coverage in high-severity areas [904][901]. Attacks on health care
and access constraints are further undermining responses: Insecurity Insight recorded more than 1,929 incidents of violence against
health care between 1 February 2021 and 12 May 2026 (66% attributed to the Myanmar Armed Forces), with at least 173 health workers
killed, 930 arrested and at least 503 health facilities damaged; recent reported incidents include bans on transporting medicines from
Pakokku and ambulances damaged by explosives [914][908]. Outside Myanmar, about 1.2 million Rohingya refugees — mostly in Cox's
Bazar — remain heavily reliant on aid, with some 150,000 new arrivals since early 2024; UNHCR and partners launched a $710.5 million
2026 appeal (hyper-prioritized) that is around 60% funded, and agencies warn that funding shortfalls, overcrowding and
extreme-weather risk are undermining food, water, health and protection services in the camps [921][900][905][909].
NFI and Shelter Needs and Current Response
IDP and displaced communities report urgent needs for shelter materials (tarpaulins and basic roofing), safe temporary shelter,
mosquito nets, medicines and other household NFIs ahead of the monsoon season [897][898][902][935]. Field reporting from
Chin-Magway and Karenni areas highlights acute gaps in immediate NFI provision — including tarpaulins, shelter kits, mosquito nets
and medicines — with frequent supply shortages and limited distribution reach leaving displaced families exposed to rain, mouldy
rations and deteriorating living conditions [898][935][902]. Local aid workers and camp-management sources report that relief
support is minimal to almost nonexistent in many areas of southern Rakhine and newly displaced sites, leaving thousands unable to
procure basic shelter materials [897][898][935]. Access and logistics represent major constraints: deliberate blockades and transport
bans — including interdictions on medicines and food from Pakokku since mid-May — and restrictions imposed by de facto authorities
impede delivery of NFIs and have forced some partners to suspend activities [898][914]. Cluster-level preparedness actions are
underway: the WASH Cluster developed a Township Prioritization Tool and UNICEF is convening AWD preparedness training (Kachin,
4–5 June 2026), while the Health Cluster is expanding prepositioning of medical supplies for rapid deployment to hard-to-reach areas
[904]. Funding shortfalls continue to constrain the overall response, with the Rohingya appeal substantially underfunded at around
60% of its reduced target, pressuring the ability to sustain shelter and basic services for refugees and adding strain to regional
humanitarian resources [900][921].
Protection
Impact on civilians
A major junta offensive and blockade along the Chin–Magway border triggered mass displacement in early June 2026, forcing roughly
14,000 people into surrounding forests and prompting about 7,000 evacuations from Mindat town plus another 7,000 from nearby
villages; Mindat's total displaced population, including long-term IDPs, was reported at about 17,000 as of 2–3 June 2026 [964][947].
Displaced families face acute shortages of shelter, food, medical supplies and exposure to monsoon rains, with camp managers
reporting moldy rations, a lack of tarpaulins and limited medical assistance for those hiding in the mountains [964]. Junta-imposed
access restrictions and blockades have stopped transport of essential goods from Pakokku since mid-May, severely constraining
deliveries of food and medicines to western Yaw region townships [964][955].
Violence against health care remains widespread, with Insecurity Insight recording more than 1,929 incidents across Myanmar
between 1 February 2021 and 12 May 2026 — approximately 66% attributed to the Myanmar Armed Forces — including at least 173
health workers killed, 930 arrested, and health facilities damaged on at least 503 occasions; 73 attacks on health care were recorded
between 1 January and 31 May 2026 [955][954][949][994]. The Myanmar Health Cluster reported intensifying airstrikes and drone
attacks in Chin, Magway, Rakhine and Sagaing that are impeding access to services and medical supply transport [954][949]. Recent
reported incidents include a 19 May landmine strike that damaged an LNGO ambulance, killing an LNGO worker and injuring patients
and staff, and 24 May artillery shelling that damaged two buildings of a functioning station hospital in Natogyi township, Mandalay
region [955].
Large-scale destruction of civilian property and forced displacement continued in May, with the Karenni Human Rights Group
documenting over 120 damaged civilian houses, vehicles and public buildings in Karenni State in May 2026 and reporting around 7,000
people displaced from Hpruso Township following arson and military operations [945].
22
Protection risks have escalated, including reported executions and arbitrary arrests — six civilians executed in Tapyin village during
May — and a patterned use of sexual violence as a tool of political repression, as noted in UN reporting on conflict-related sexual
violence in Myanmar [964][969].
Rohingya populations remain heavily dependent on humanitarian aid and at heightened risk from funding shortfalls; UNHCR and
partners launched a $710.5 million appeal in late May/early June and warned the response was only around 60% funded, jeopardizing
food, shelter, health and protection services for refugees linked to the Myanmar crisis [956][944]. Health partners report major
coverage gaps: as of Q1 2026 they were providing services in 106 of 227 prioritized townships (47%), while many high-severity (level 4)
townships — largely outside junta control — remain inaccessible to partners, limiting essential service delivery [954].
Factors Driving protection risks
Ongoing military operations, intensified airstrikes, drone strikes and widespread use of heavy weapons have escalated civilian harm
and severely impeded access to health care and medical logistics across multiple states, including Chin, Magway, Rakhine, Sagaing,
Kachin, Karenni and northern Shan [949][954][955]. Systematic attacks on health care are a persistent driver of protection risk, with
armed-group activity, landmines and unsafe explosive storage also producing direct civilian casualties and disrupting aid operations
— highlighted by cross-border landmine and mortar casualties near Bangladesh in late May–early June 2026, and a large accidental
explosives blast in Namhkam at end-May 2026 linked to stored mining explosives [955][980][966][961][960].
Arbitrary arrests, detention and intensified digital repression — including revocation of publishing licences on 11 May 2026, documented
arrests for online expression, and reported deaths of political prisoners in late May 2026 — are shrinking civic space and producing
detention-related protection harms [950][943]. Targeting of livelihoods (including reported attacks on rice fields and widespread
village burnings), massive internal displacement and reduced humanitarian funding are driving acute economic deprivation and
dependency, with refugee and displaced populations including Rohingya facing heightened vulnerability and about 150,000 new
arrivals from Rakhine since early 2024 relying on aid [950][951][944][948].
Legal and institutional weaknesses and information blackouts are erecting barriers to protection and justice, while constrained
humanitarian access is illustrated by health partners reaching services in only 47% of the 227 prioritized townships and reporting
interventions in just 35% of townships categorised as extremely deprived for health [954][950][943]. These intersecting drivers are
producing mounting civilian casualties, repeated displacement, restricted access to essential services and erosion of basic
protections, with recent localized displacements — including more than 5,000 people in Tanintharyi since mid-May 2026 and roughly
12,000 displaced in western Bago since April 2026 — underscoring the scale of need [942][941][949].
Psychological and mental health impacts
The Assistance Association for Political Prisoners (AAPP) provides psychological support and online mental-health/self-rehabilitation
training for former political prisoners experiencing PTSD, depression and anxiety, and delivers training intended to reduce
mental-health misconceptions and link released prisoners with professional services [965]. AAPP figures indicate the regime continues
to hold more than 22,000 political prisoners while nearly 9,000 have been released, indicating a large population with potential MHPSS
needs [965]. While civil society groups and ICRC assistance (e.g., covering travel costs to prisons) provide some support to detainees
and families, reporting highlights persistent gaps in comprehensive MHPSS coverage, access to professionals and targeted services for
vulnerable groups including former prisoners, displaced populations and survivors of violence [965].
Violence against health care has degraded access to mental-health services, and WHO's Surveillance System for Attacks on Health
Care recorded 38 verified attacks between 1 January and 31 May 2026; Health Cluster analysis shows "psychological violence" featured
in 11% of reported incidents in early 2026, signalling direct threats to both provider and patient mental well-being and added barriers to
safe care [955][954][994]. The Health Cluster has planned SSA awareness sessions to encourage incident reporting by partners,
reflecting recognition of reporting and monitoring gaps that affect protection and MHPSS planning [954].
Intensifying conflict and displacement — including the roughly 14,000 people forced into mountains and camps along the
Chin–Magway border in mid-May–early June 2026 — have left displaced populations facing acute shortages of shelter, food and
medicine in monsoon conditions, exacerbating trauma and psychosocial distress [964]. Local incident reporting further documents
injured families facing high treatment costs, displacement and no external support, illustrating economic barriers to recovery and
gaps in psychosocial assistance for survivors of attacks and shelling [959][982].
Protection Needs and Current Response
Protection needs across Myanmar remain acute, with escalating violence, constrained partner presence and access impediments
leaving high-severity areas and displaced populations severely under-served. Key figures as of Q1/mid-2026 include:
- Health partners providing services in 106 of 227 prioritized townships (47%) as of Q1 2026 [954].
- Of 86 townships classified as severity level 4 for health, partners submitted interventions from only 30 townships (35%) — many
high-severity areas remain inaccessible [954].
- More than 5,000 people displaced in Tanintharyi since mid-May 2026 and around 12,000 in western Bago since April, many
sheltering in forests or makeshift sites and facing acute shortages of food and basic supplies [942][952].
- More than 3,000 IDPs in southern Rakhine (Taungup, Thandwe, Gwa) face severe food insecurity, minimal humanitarian access
and inadequate shelter ahead of the monsoon season [952].
On the humanitarian response side, the Health Cluster is scaling reporting and monitoring through SSA awareness sessions to
incentivize partners to report attacks, and expanding prepositioning of medical supplies for rapid deployment to hard-to-reach areas
[954].
23
UNICEF is supporting AWD/cholera preparedness training in Kachin on 4–5 June 2026, and UNFPA released 29 Inter-Agency
Reproductive Health kits to support SRH services [954]. However, registration obstacles imposed by de facto authorities are forcing
some NGOs to cease activities, and checkpoints and movement restrictions — including bans on transporting medicines from Pakokku
to villages in Magway Region — are further constraining protection and assistance delivery [954][994]. The killing of an LNGO worker
and damage to an ambulance on 19 May 2026 continue to underscore risks to frontline responders and patients [955][994]. Overall,
persistent gaps in protection monitoring, case management and safe shelter, combined with partner coverage under 50% of
prioritized townships, leave the most vulnerable populations critically exposed [954][952].
Child Protection concerns
A large explosion in Namhkam, northern Shan State (late May–early June 2026) killed dozens including children and injured many,
creating urgent protection and displacement needs for affected children and families [961][966][988][960]. Cross-border spillover
violence has directly harmed children near the Bangladesh border, including the reported killing of a child by an abandoned mortar on
2 June 2026 [980]. Severe food shortages among more than 3,000 IDPs in southern Rakhine (Taungup, Thandwe, Gwa) have driven
children to beg for food, signalling rising child protection and child-labour risks [952].
UNHCR and partners warn that about 1.2 million Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh face reduced assistance, limited access to
education and heightened protection risks, with nearly 900 Rohingya reported missing or dead at sea in 2025 — factors that increase
vulnerabilities for children and adolescents [944][963][948][956]. Intensified displacement inside Myanmar — including more than
5,000 people in Tanintharyi since mid-May 2026 and around 12,000 in western Bago since April — is exposing children to interrupted
services and protection threats [942]. The presence of armed groups and indicators of recruitment and criminal activity around
camps and borderlands raise risks of recruitment, exploitation and gender-based abuses affecting children and young people
[980][969].
Disruptions to health and education services — including large gaps in partner coverage of high-severity townships and measles
preparedness concerns in border areas with many previously unvaccinated children — further undermine child protection by reducing
access to vaccination, learning and child-friendly services [954][949].
Violence against women and girls
Sexual violence is being used as a tactic of political violence in Myanmar, contributing to patterns of conflict-related sexual violence
documented by the UN Secretary-General's report and subsequent monitoring analyses [969]. The Burmese Women's Union
documented 44 women killed in April amid junta air and ground attacks, indicating heightened protection risks for women and girls,
while arrests of women — 114 women among 374 people detained in a recent MIP tally — and digital repression and communications
blackouts are increasing barriers to reporting GBV and to women's ability to reach services [943][950]. At least 53 maternal health
services have been reported damaged or disrupted as part of the broader pattern of attacks on health care [955][994][949][954].
UNFPA and health partners have maintained GBV/SRH response capacity where possible: UNFPA released 29 Inter-Agency
Reproductive Health (IARH) kits to partners and organized two Clinical Management of Rape (CMR) capacity-building sessions (one
virtual, one in-person) around 1 June 2026, while SRH delivery has relied largely on mobile and community-based approaches to reach
underserved populations [954]. Funding cuts and blocked humanitarian access continue to weaken prevention, monitoring and
survivor assistance; UNHCR warned in early June 2026 that women and girls among Rohingya refugees are particularly affected by
reduced aid and service shortfalls [956][948].

Pregnant and Lactating Women
Attacks on health care have been extensive since the 2021 coup, with 1,929 incidents recorded up to 12 May 2026 and at least 53
maternal health services reported damaged, disrupted, or otherwise affected, reducing access to care for pregnant women, mothers
and newborns [1009][1007]. Insecurity Insight reported 73 incidents affecting health care between 1 January and 31 May 2026, while
WHO's SSA recorded 38 verified attacks in the same period, highlighting an ongoing surge in hostile incidents that undermine maternal
health service delivery [1006]. Intensified airstrikes and drone use across Chin, Magway, Rakhine, Sagaing, Kachin, Karenni and northern
Shan have severely impeded access to health care and the transport of medical supplies needed for maternal services [1006].
Conflict-related restrictions on movement and blockades have further disrupted medical supply chains — for example, junta
checkpoints banned transport of medicines and food from Pakokku on 13 May 2026, and two buildings of a station hospital were
damaged by artillery on 24 May 2026 — further reducing access to maternal care [1009].
Health partners reported providing services in 106 of 227 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan priority townships (47%) during Q1
2026, and interventions were reported from only 30 of 86 townships categorized as "extremely deprived" (35%), indicating large gaps in
coverage where pregnant and breastfeeding women are likely to be underserved [1013]. Sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services
have mainly been delivered through mobile and community-based approaches to reach underserved populations, and UNFPA
released 29 Inter-Agency Reproductive Health (IARH) kits to SRH partners, including supplies for referral hospitals providing
Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (CEmONC) [1013]. Internally displaced and remote populations report critical
gaps relevant to maternal health: clinics absent or visited infrequently, long travel times to the nearest health centre, shortages of
medicines, and rising malaria and other infectious disease risks that compound vulnerabilities for pregnant women and infants in IDP
camps [1015].
24
In the Rohingya refugee response in Bangladesh, WFP reported delivering nutrition services in April 2026 that reached 43,700 pregnant
and breastfeeding women, underscoring high nutrition needs among displaced pregnant and lactating populations [1010]. Patterns of
conflict-related sexual violence and worsening violations of women's rights have been documented in Myanmar, with monitoring
groups reporting increases in violence against women and women killed in attacks, creating protection risks that intersect with
maternal health needs [1055][1019]. Operational constraints — including NGO registration barriers, intensified conflict limiting access,
and connectivity and reporting challenges — continue to impede partners' ability to deliver and monitor maternal health services,
prompting Health Cluster plans for SSA awareness sessions, expanded prepositioning of medical supplies, and further facility and
market assessments to support service continuity [1013].
Adolescents and Youth
Airstrikes, drone strikes and shelling have regularly targeted villages and schools across Myanmar, driving displacement and
interrupting education for children and adolescents [1019][1006]. Intensified operations since mid-May 2026 displaced more than
5,000 people in Tanintharyi and left around 12,000 displaced in western Bago since April, with constrained humanitarian access and
elevated needs that undermine schooling and youth livelihoods [1014]. In southern Rakhine/Arakan State, over 3,000 IDPs in Taungup,
Thandwe and Gwa face acute food insecurity and minimal relief, and aid workers report an increase in displaced children begging as
households lack income or assistance [1012].
Rohingya refugees and around 150,000 new arrivals from Rakhine face limited education and economic opportunities in camps;
UNHCR warned funding cuts are threatening essential services and prospects for return are fading, while WFP and partners note
continued progress in refugee education but persistent funding shortfalls that affect household stability [1008][1010]. Reports describe
growing militarisation of the Cox's Bazar camps and surrounding areas, with armed recruitment and criminal economies identified as
risks inside and around the camps [1022]. Psychosocial support is provided by groups such as the Assistance Association for Political
Prisoners (AAPP), which offers psychological support and training to former political prisoners, but widespread attacks on health care
and restricted partner access are eroding the availability of mental-health and other services for affected youth populations
[1023][1009][1013].
People with Disabilities
According to UNHCR, persons with disabilities among the roughly 1.2 million Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh are among the most
vulnerable and are disproportionately affected by sharp cuts in humanitarian and development assistance [1005][1008][1004]. In May
2026, the UN and the Government of Bangladesh launched an appeal for $710.5 million to meet urgent needs for Rohingya refugees
and host communities, but the appeal was only about 60% funded and 26% lower than last year, increasing the risk of reduced
healthcare, education and protection services that persons with disabilities rely on [1008][1004]. UNHCR cautioned that maintaining
only minimal levels of assistance could lead to more complex and costly humanitarian consequences for the most vulnerable groups,
explicitly naming persons with disabilities among those at heightened risk [1005][1004].
Elderly
In Karenni State, elderly IDP residents with chronic conditions such as hypertension and diabetes are unable to afford medicines and
face extremely limited access to clinics and mobile health teams, with outbreaks and medicine shortages reported at the onset of the
rainy season in May 2026 [1015]. The Health Cluster (1 June 2026) reported that intensified airstrikes and drone attacks are severely
impeding access to health care and transport of medical supplies, and announced plans to expand prepositioning of medical
supplies, conduct SSA awareness sessions, and deliver additional noncommunicable-disease-in-emergencies workshops to support
NCD care for older people [1013][1006].
Blockades and checkpoint restrictions since mid-May — including bans on transporting medicines and food from Pakokku and a junta
blockade cutting supplies to western Yaw region since 14 May — have left displaced communities, including older people, without
medicines and basic supplies [1009][1021]. Displacement, reduced humanitarian presence and mobility constraints documented in
late May–early June 2026 have increased protection risks and social isolation for older people across multiple regions and IDP sites
[1014][1012][1004]. UNHCR and partners warn that funding cuts and a hyper-prioritised 2026 appeal (around 60% funded) are reducing
services for Rohingya refugees and other displaced populations, with older people explicitly identified among the most affected
vulnerable groups [1004][1005].
Displaced
Key displacement and refugee figures reported in early June 2026 include the following:
- More than 5,000 people displaced in Tanintharyi Region after intensified operations since mid-May 2026 [1014].
- Around 12,000 people remain displaced in western Bago Region since April 2026 amid continued airstrikes and insecurity [1014].
- Roughly 14,000 residents evacuated Mindat town and nearby villages since mid-May 2026, joining about 10,000 long-term IDPs
for an estimated 17,000 people displaced in Mindat township [1021].
- Since renewed fighting in November 2023, about 600,000 people have been displaced across Arakan (Rakhine) State, with
pockets — such as over 3,000 IDPs in southern Arakan townships — facing acute food insecurity and minimal humanitarian
assistance [1012].
- Some 1.2 million Rohingya refugees remain in Bangladesh (mostly in Cox's Bazar), including approximately 150,000 new arrivals
since early 2024; a 2026 UN-led appeal for their needs totals US$710.5 million and was reported about 60% funded at the time of
reporting [1008][1004][1005][1016][1026].
25
Displaced households are sheltering in forested and mountainous areas, with many living in temporary makeshift camps with
inadequate shelter supplies (lack of tarpaulins and roofing), limited income sources and rising reliance on begging and irregular
coping strategies ahead of the monsoon season [1012][1021]. Livelihood opportunities are scarce in displacement-affected areas; local
economies have collapsed in many frontline areas and displaced families report virtually no casual labour or formal employment,
increasing food insecurity and dependence on shrinking aid supplies [1012].
Health and basic services are severely constrained: health partners reported providing services in 106 of 227 prioritized townships
(47%), and only 30 of 86 townships classed as severity level 4 have partner interventions (35%), reflecting major access gaps in
conflict-affected areas [1013]. Overcrowded IDP sites are already seeing surges in infectious diseases (malaria, dengue, AWD, mumps
and skin infections), driven by poor WASH, medicine shortages and limited mobility to reach clinics [1015][1013]. Attacks on health care
and intensified use of heavy weapons, airstrikes and drones — with hundreds of documented incidents since 2021 and dozens reported
in early 2026 — have damaged facilities, killed and arrested health workers, and further undermined service delivery and disease
surveillance [1009][1006][1007].
WFP reported adapting targeting in the Bangladesh refugee operation and supported 1.13 million Rohingya in Cox's Bazar in April 2026
while continuing to face operational strains during program changes [1010]. Prospects for safe return remain limited: UNHCR and
partners report that ongoing conflict, persecution and insecurity inside Myanmar continue to prevent voluntary, safe and dignified
return for refugees, contributing to secondary movement and dangerous sea crossings — nearly 900 Rohingya were reported dead or
missing in regional sea crossings in 2025 — as people seek alternatives [1008][1004][1005][1016][1026].
Protection risks for displaced populations include targeted military offensives, blockades that cut supply routes (notably transport
blockages from Pakokku toward western Yaw region since 14 May 2026), intensified air and drone attacks, and shrinking humanitarian
access that limits assistance and heightens exposure to violence and rights violations [1021][1006][1014]. Rohingya in Malaysia lack
formal legal status and face barriers to legal employment, education and basic services, even as Malaysia in 2026 rolled out a refugee
registration system that had registered some 4,010 refugees (many detained at immigration depots) for biometric profiling and
potential labour matching [1037]. Funding shortfalls combined with access constraints and sustained conflict thus compound
protection, health, shelter and livelihood gaps for both internally displaced people inside Myanmar and refugees from Myanmar in
neighbouring countries [1008][1013][1012][1006].
Minorities
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees remain in Bangladesh, with roughly 150,000 new arrivals since early 2024, continuing to rely heavily
on humanitarian assistance; women and girls, people with disabilities and older people are disproportionately affected by the crisis
[1004][1008]. The UN-led appeal to meet urgent needs for Rohingya refugees and host communities totalled about $710.5 million for
2026 and was reported at roughly 60% funded — a funding request 26% lower than the previous year — raising concerns about cuts to
essential services [1008][1010]. WFP introduced a food-insecurity-based Targeting and Prioritization Exercise effective 1 April 2026 that
adjusts monthly entitlements by household food security while maintaining coverage for all households, and in April WFP reached 1.13
million refugees in Cox's Bazar and 28,000 in Bhasan Char with general food assistance [1010]. With prospects for safe return fading,
many Rohingya resort to perilous sea journeys; 2025 was recorded as the deadliest year for such crossings, with nearly 900 reported
dead or missing in the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal [1008].
Violence against health care is widespread and sustained: Insecurity Insight recorded 1,929 incidents affecting health care in Myanmar
between 1 February 2021 and 12 May 2026, with 66% attributed to the Myanmar Armed Forces, at least 173 health workers killed, 930
arrested, and health facilities damaged on at least 503 occasions; the growing use of drones has further endangered services [1009].
In Rakhine (Arakan) State, renewed conflict since November 2023 has displaced around 600,000 people, and a junta-imposed
blockade has disrupted transport and supply chains, while more than 3,000 IDPs in southern townships face acute food insecurity
amid very limited aid presence [1012].
Sexual violence has been documented as part of the repertoire of political violence in Myanmar, used to intimidate, punish and target
communities along shifting frontlines and on ethnic grounds [1055]. Digital repression and communications blackouts — alongside
arrests targeting online expression — disproportionately endanger women, women's rights defenders and activists, and hamper
communication with families in areas such as Rakhine, increasing exclusion and protection risks [1027]. International accountability
measures relevant to Rohingya abuses include proceedings before the International Court of Justice and an Argentinian arrest
warrant issued in 2025 against Myanmar's military leader Min Aung Hlaing for alleged crimes against the Rohingya [1034].
